Check the wiring before onboarding. edge/tools/i2c_hub_test.py is the I2C hub bench test the bench template comes from. It runs on the board itself and changes nothing on the platform. Set the lines of its CONFIG block (SHT45_CH, SCD30_CH, LUX_CH, the pins) to the ports the cables are in, then run it with Thonny (F5) or mpremote connect <port> run edge/tools/i2c_hub_test.py. It checks that only the hub answers on the root bus, that each sensor answers on its own channel and on no other (a cable in the wrong port prints a hint naming the port it found), reads the SHT45 and the SCD30, and runs 20 hub-switching cycles; it ends with ALL PASS or a list of failures. Use the same channels on the wiring screen. The test sets the SCD30 to measure every 2 s, as the board firmware does. A test file in the repository (tests/test_i2c_hub_test.py) keeps the script's channels and pins equal to the bench template's.

Onboarding a slot again. When the slot's board was onboarded on screen before, the screen opens with the wiring its provisioning record holds.

The questions instead. Answer one sensor at a time (questions) keeps the older way, one sensor and its pins at a time. It offers the sensors that sit on their own pins (SCD40/41, SCD30, DS18B20, water level), not the SHT45, the SEN0562 or the hub. Boards onboarded that way keep working unchanged.

In a terminal. --wiring FILE takes the wiring from a document (or a board template file) and --board-template NAME from a template, with no questions; both are checked before the board is touched. Without either, a terminal run asks the questions.

A board that is not an ESP32-S3. The screen's pin table is the ESP32-S3's, and the reference pins GPIO 8 and 9 are the SPI flash pins of an original ESP32 ("GPIO8 is wired to the module's SPI flash. Driving it crashes the board."). When the plugged-in chip differs from the one the wiring was checked against, the run checks it again against the real chip after probing, and stops before the erase if it cannot work there. For such a board choose Answer one sensor at a time (questions), or give --wiring FILE with board.variant set to the chip (for example esp32c3) and no board.part.

The accepted wiring goes into the provisioning record ("wiring"), and each sensor becomes one component record of the device, with its driver, address, bus pins, hub and channel, and the tags it publishes. A saved board template records who saved it and when (saved_by, saved_at, and replaced_at when it replaced one).

On the board, all sensors on one bus share it; a hub channel is opened before each sensor is read, and any channel open on another hub of the same bus is closed first, so only one channel is ever on the wire. A sensor that fails does not stop the board: see the health message below.

Health and test messages

Besides its readings, a board sends two kinds of message of its own. Both carry the fields of a reading (unit_code, zone_code, msg_type, timestamp, device_id, device_dns, tag), plus the board's network address ip and its MAC address mac (each null when the board cannot read it), and no value or unit.

MessageTopicStored asWhenExtra fields
Healthmedcea/<UNIT>/<ZONE>/sense/_healthHBA SENSE board, at start-up and whenever a sensor goes down or comes back.sensors: one entry per sensor, {"id", "ok", "err"}; err is the reason in at most 80 characters, or null.
Test…/sense/_test (SENSE), …/control_setpoint/_test (CONTROL)TSEvery board once at start-up, right after it first connects to the broker; and from the host on request (Sending a test message).source: board-boot, wizard or cli; firmware: the MicroPython release, for example 1.29.0. A test sent from the host also carries "sent_from": "host".

A CONTROL board sends no health message: it may publish only under its control_setpoint topics, which is also why its test message goes there.

A sensor that fails no longer restarts the board (since 6 November 2026; before, a SENSE board on which no sensor answered restarted every 15 seconds and never connected). The board connects, says in its health message which sensor is down and why, keeps publishing the others, reads a sensor that stopped answering again at every cycle, and sets up one that failed at start-up again every 10 minutes. Only the broker restarts it: unreachable when the board starts, or refusing ten publish cycles in a row. An SCD30 is given its first minute to warm up before "no reading yet" counts as down. A cycle with nothing to publish keeps the connection alive with a ping.

How the type is set. The ingest flow in Node-RED takes the type from the topic, not from the message: exactly <root>/<UNIT>/<ZONE>/sense/_health is stored as HB, and exactly …/sense/_test or …/control_setpoint/_test as TS, whatever type the message names. So a test message can never be stored as a reading. A message on any other topic that names HB or TS is dropped, with the line dropped: TS is not allowed on <topic> in Node-RED's log. A CONTROL board's pin report is one topic level longer, so a pin labelled _test is still stored as a report (SP).

Where to find them.

  • MQTT Explorer (engineer): under the slot's topic, the tags _health and _test, as they arrive.
  • The database: medcea.measurement, with msg_type HB or TS and the whole message in msg. The Run Monitor, the Grafana dashboards and the measurement views read readings (AP), commands (CT) and reports (SP) only, so neither type appears there. An engineer can look with Grafana's Explore, for example SELECT measure_timestamp, device_dns, msg->>'source' AS source, msg->>'sent_from' AS sent_from FROM medcea.measurement WHERE msg_type = 'TS' ORDER BY measure_timestamp DESC LIMIT 20; qa, qp and auditor through a Database Management export of the telemetry.

Both types are stored once ./apps/database/deploy.sh (migration 009) and ./apps/node-red/deploy.sh have run. Before that the database refuses them, as it did every _health message until 6 November 2026, and Node-RED logs the refused insert.

Sending a test message

A test message sent from the host, as the board, proves the board's path to the platform without touching the board: its broker credential, its topic rights, the broker's TLS name and the ingest flow together. It connects with the board's own credential, read from its provisioning record, over the boards' TLS port, and publishes one TS message on the topic the board itself uses. The password never appears on the command line, on screen or in a log.

  • In the wizard. After a run that registered a board, the page shows Send test message. Only the person who started the run may use it; their onboarding role is checked again first. The wizard takes the board from the run, never from the page. It answers "Sent at <time> on <topic>; look for tag _test in the MQTT Explorer.", or "Not sent: <reason>" (for example not authorised, the broker's answer to a credential it does not know: a board marked Inactive or onboarded again since). One message every 5 seconds: "One test message every 5 seconds — try again in a moment." A run that did not register a board offers no button. A --ui run's page stops a few seconds after the run ends; use the command below instead.
  • In a terminal on the platform host: ./edge/flash-device.sh --send-test unit02-s-zone01. No USB and no sign-in; it needs the board's record edge/provisioned/<name>.json, the platform's certificate authority .ca/ca.crt, and the broker address and name from config.env (or --mqtt-host, --mqtt-port, --mqtt-tls-name, the only options it takes with it). It prints one line such as {"ok":true,"topic":"medcea/UNIT02/ZONE01/sense/_test",…} and exits 0 when sent, 1 when the network or the broker refused, 2 when the record cannot be used (no record, a board onboarded with --unregistered, no broker credential, or a record the board left behind: when a board is moved to another slot or onboarded again under another name, its old record stays in edge/provisioned/ but its old credential is retired, so the command refuses it and names the board's later record, for example "this record is superseded: the same board was onboarded later as unit01-s-zone01 … Send as unit01-s-zone01.").
  • In medcea.sh: ./medcea.sh → Edge devices → Send a test message as a board lists the registered boards that have a record, only the latest record of each board (by its MAC address), and runs the command above.

"Sent" means the broker accepted the message. The broker also acknowledges a message its access rules refuse, and drops it silently, so look for tag _test in the MQTT Explorer, or the TS row in the database, to see it arrived.

Each test message is a TS row in medcea.measurement; one sent from the host says "sent_from": "host" and "source": "wizard" or "cli". The wizard's log names the board and the person who sent it, never a credential. Engineers sending a test message from the MQTT Explorer is planned and needs an approved change of the access policy first (see the decision record).

Testing a CONTROL board: commissioning

After a CONTROL board is onboarded, an engineer can check its wiring by sending commands to it by hand from the MQTT Explorer. The broker allows that only while the board's unit is flagged for commissioning (test mode) and has no run in progress:

  1. Make sure no run is running or scheduled on the unit; flagging is refused while one is.
  2. In the Configuration UI's Units tab, click Flag for commissioning… on the unit, give the reason (for example "relay test of the new CONTROL board in zone 2") and click Propose.
  3. Ask a qa person to approve it. Within about 15 seconds of the approval, the broker accepts your messages to the unit's control topics. The MQTT Explorer's Your rights note does not change: it lists your role's pattern, medcea/+/+/control/#, for every unit.
  4. Send the test commands to one concrete topic, for example medcea/UNIT01/ZONE01/control/<tag> (never the pattern itself: the page refuses + and #), and watch the board's control_setpoint reports. Clicking the topic in the left-hand list shows your message as the broker delivered it.
  5. Click End commissioning… on the unit when you are done. It applies at once; runs can start on the unit again, and qa reviews it afterwards.

The full procedure, the refusals and who sees what are in commissioning a unit.

Replacing a board

Use this when a board fails and a new board takes its place in the same slot. maintenance and engineer may do it.

  1. In the Devices tab, press Edit on the old board, set Status to Inactive and save. The slot becomes free, and within about 15 seconds the broker refuses the old board.
  2. Plug the new board into the platform host and start onboarding.
  3. Pick the same role and the now free slot. Wire it, flash it and let it register as usual.

The registration updates the slot's existing record in place. The record keeps its id, gets the new board's serial number, becomes Active again, and its components are replaced with the ones just chosen. The board gets the same name as before and a new broker password.

To re-flash the same board in its own slot (a firmware update, new pins), onboard it again without deactivating it. The run sees that the board is already in this slot and updates its record in place. The broker password changes.

Replacement is recorded in the slot history as replaced, with the old and the new serial number and the person who did it. Changing the serial number also deactivates the old board's broker credential.

Moving a board

A board's record follows the board, because its serial number (the MAC address) is unique. To move a board to another slot, start onboarding with the board plugged in and pick the new slot. When the run reads the board's MAC address, it finds the existing record and asks:

this board is already registered as unit01-s-zone01 - UNIT01 / ZONE01 (SENSE).
Move this board from unit01-s-zone01 to UNIT01 / ZONE02?
  • Yes moves the record to the new slot. The board takes the new slot's name, its components are replaced, and the old slot becomes free. If the new slot holds an older inactive record with the same name, that record is renamed <name>-<id> and kept inactive.
  • No stops the run before anything is erased or written.

The question comes after the board is probed and before the erase, because that is the first moment both the board and the target slot are known. A run started with -y never moves a board: it stops and asks you to onboard interactively.

maintenance may move a board only into a slot that already has an inactive record. Moving a board into a slot that never had one is an engineer's change.

A move is recorded in the slot history as moved, with the old and new zone, role and name.

MQTT credentials per board

The broker admits nobody anonymously. Each registered board has its own credential:

  • User name: the board's name, for example unit02-c-zone02.
  • Password: a fresh random password minted at every onboarding, so re-flashing a board changes it. The password goes onto the board and into its provisioning record. The platform database stores only its hash.
  • Access by role. The broker lets a SENSE board publish only under its own slot's sense/ topics. It lets a CONTROL board receive only its own slot's control/ topics and publish only its own control_setpoint/ topics.

A sidecar next to the broker rebuilds the broker's password and access files from the database every 15 seconds. Two things follow from that:

  • Deactivation revokes within about 15 seconds. When a device is marked Inactive (devices are retired, never deleted), its credential drops out at the next rebuild. The broker then refuses its next connection and denies its publishes.
  • The first connections of a new board may be refused. The board boots before it is registered. Until the registration lands and the next rebuild picks it up, which takes up to about 15 seconds, the broker refuses the board. The board restarts after 10 seconds and tries again, so this clears by itself.

A board that is not registered (the run was refused, the board had no IP, or --no-register) has a password that the broker does not know, so it cannot publish. Onboard it again once the cause is fixed.

Boards flashed before broker authentication existed have no credential. Re-onboard them.

Boards connect over TLS only (since 5 November 2026), on the broker's LAN port 31884. The board checks the broker's certificate before it sends its password: it must be signed by the platform's own certificate authority, which onboarding copies to the board, and carry the name mqtt.<domain>. So the password never crosses the network in clear, and a machine that pretends to be the broker is refused. The certificate's dates are checked too: a board whose clock is not set yet (no answer from the internet time server at start-up) asks for the time once more and otherwise restarts and tries again. The plain port 31883 is closed, so a board onboarded before that date cannot connect until it is onboarded again. The platform's own services connect inside the cluster on port 1883. With IAM_MQTT_PERSON=true that port accepts no person's credential: the MQTT Explorer's personal credentials work only on the broker's WebSocket listener, behind the Explorer's sign-in (see MQTT Explorer). The shared mqtt-explorer account was removed on 1 November 2026 and is refused on both ports. Watch the board in the MQTT Explorer instead (the onboarding summary says so while IAM_MQTT_PERSON is true).

TLS protects the connection, not the board. The WiFi passphrase and the MQTT password sit in plain text on the board's flash. Anyone holding the board can read them. WebREPL also stays on after onboarding: anyone who reaches port 8266 with the board's WebREPL password gets a full Python prompt and the board's files. Treat a lost board as a lost credential and mark it Inactive.

Slot history and what gets recorded

The database keeps an append-only history of where every board has been. A database trigger writes it on every change to a device record, whoever makes the change: onboarding, the Devices tab or a direct database change. Nobody can edit or delete the history, and it outlives a deleted device record.

EventWhen
placedA device record was created.
movedIts zone or role changed.
renamedOnly its name changed, for example after a unit or zone code was renamed and the slot re-onboarded.
replacedA different board (serial number) took over the record.
removedThe record was deleted.

Each event holds the board's serial number, the zone, role and name before and after, the time, and who made the change: their account, person id, name, platform role and source. A re-flash in place with no change of slot, name or board adds no event.

For each onboarding the platform records: the device record and its components, stamped with the person whose sign-in the run used; the slot history event; the board's credential hash; and on the host, edge/provisioned/<name>.json with the MAC address, chip, firmware file and its SHA-256, MicroPython version, tool versions, the IP at onboarding, the host login that flashed it, the Keycloak account that registered it and, for a SENSE board wired on screen or with --wiring/--board-template, its wiring. Every stored measurement is stamped with the zone its board was in when the reading arrived.

maintenance and engineer may read the slot history. auditor and qa may read it and export it from Database Management.

Adding a sensor type

The wizard's questions are data, not code. The SENSE questions come from edge/templates/esp32-sense.json and the CONTROL questions from edge/templates/esp32-control.json. Each sensor entry gives its name, the tags it publishes, and the parameters to ask, with the reference build's wiring as defaults. Neither flash-device.sh nor the wizard page changes when an entry is added.

A sensor also needs code on the board to read it: a reading function in the board application (edge/src/app/cea_sensors.py). If that function already exists, the template entry is all that is needed. A new kind of sensor needs a new reading function, which is a developer's change made through the normal review.

A sensor offered on the wiring screen has, in its template entry, a bus block (its addresses and fastest clock), its power rails, the quantities it measures with their default tags, and the name of its picture in edge/templates/parts/; on the board it needs a set-up and a read function in edge/src/app/cea_sense.py. The pictures of the Adafruit boards come from Adafruit's Fritzing library (CC BY-SA 3.0, listed in edge/templates/parts/ATTRIBUTION.md), converted with edge/tools/import-fritzing.py.

New device types in the onboarding page work the same way. Each tile is an entry in edge/catalog.json. An entry whose script is missing or not executable is shown as unavailable.

Bench mode

./edge/flash-device.sh --unregistered

This brings a board up on WiFi with no platform identity, for a bench with no platform deployed. It asks no slot, ships no application, writes nothing to the database and needs no sign-in. The board is named cea-un-<mac6> and has no MQTT credential, so it cannot connect to the broker. It joins WiFi and keeps WebREPL open, so the warning in MQTT credentials per board applies to it too. To give it a slot later, onboard it normally. Nothing has to be undone.

A registered run also offers to continue unregistered when the platform database does not answer or no sign-in is possible. If you accept, the board ends up the same as with --unregistered.

--no-register is different: it flashes the board for a slot with its application and pins, but does not write the device record. The slot still reads as free, and the broker refuses the board until it is onboarded again with registration.

When onboarding is refused

The wizard explains a refusal from the platform database in plain words:

The wizard saysWhat to do
this role may not onboard boards (permission denied)Ask an administrator for the engineer or maintenance role.
no platform role, or two own rolesAsk an administrator to fix the account in the User Manager.
anonymous request refused, or the sign-in token was refusedSign in again and re-run.
the token expired during the requestRe-run. The slot's record is updated in place.
config-api has no JWT keyAdministrator: run ./deploy-infra.sh, then ./apps/frontend/deploy.sh.
the code expired before the sign-in was finishedRe-run for a new code. If Keycloak said the account is disabled, the access request is still pending or the account was deactivated.
no free SENSE (or CONTROL) slotMark the existing device Inactive, or add a zone in the Units tab.
not offered: ... is not a legal hostnameRename the unit or zone code in the Units tab.

The run checks your sign-in again when it checks the board, just before the erase and just before the registration. If your session has ended (you signed out, or your account was deactivated), the run pauses and asks the same person to sign in again: the browser page sends you to the sign-in page, and a terminal run shows a new code. The run waits up to 15 minutes. If nobody signs in by then, a run that has not yet erased the board stops with "Nothing was erased".

If you no longer hold engineer or maintenance (the roles the access policy admits to onboarding), the run stops before the erase. After the erase it skips the registration instead, and the board stays unregistered.

Access control and records

This chapter is for quality staff (qa, qc, qp), auditors and thesis examiners. It describes the one access policy that says who may do what, the layers that enforce it, the decisions that need a second person, and the records the platform keeps of every change. It ends with the known gaps and the decision record. It describes the platform as deployed on 31 October 2026, including the Approvals tab and unit commissioning (branch feat/approve-commission). The current value of each switch is shown by ./health-check.sh and in each access review.

The access policy: one source

Every access right on the platform comes from one policy. Its factory file is apps/iam/policy/defaults.yaml; since IAM 4.2a the policy in force is the database's applied version (version 1 is that factory file), which every deploy reads through state/policy-applied.yaml (see The applied access policy). A compiler reads it and produces the database grants, the sign-in gate of each web host, the route table every service checks and the network policies. Grafana, the AI workbench, the device onboarding wizard and pgAdmin sign people in themselves; their own sign-in settings are compiled from it too. The compiler refuses to compile a policy that breaks one of its invariants.

The policy is a matrix. Rows are resource groups: a set of tables, API routes, web pages and MQTT topics that belong together, such as "Recipes and recipe-to-unit assignment" or "Telemetry". Columns are the eleven platform roles. A cell lists the access levels a role holds on a group. A role not listed in a row holds nothing there. Every account has exactly one platform role.

Roles

RoleName in the UIWhat the role is for
operatorCultivation OperatorRuns the cultivation day to day in the units assigned to them.
production_managerProduction Manager (Process Owner)Prepares and starts runs, assigns approved recipes and parameter sets to units. Holds everything an operator holds, in every unit.
maintenanceMaintenance and CalibrationReplaces and calibrates boards and sensors in existing slots.
qcQuality Control AnalystTests product and records lab results. Offered, but tagged "not yet in use".
qaQuality AssuranceIndependent approver of configuration, access decisions and policy changes. Also holds everything auditor holds.
qpQualified / Responsible PersonReleases the output of a completed run; creates and changes nothing. Offered, but tagged "not yet in use".
engineerAutomation EngineerBuilds master data, devices, recipes, controllers, flows and dashboards as drafts that qa approves.
bio_scientistBio-process ScientistReads recipes, controllers and telemetry (no export); works in the AI workbench.
control_scientistControl and AI ScientistReads controllers, parameter sets and telemetry (no export); develops algorithms in the AI workbench.
adminSystem AdministratorKeeps the platform running and administers accounts and the policy, without access to regulated or history content.
auditorAuditor / InspectorReads and exports records, configuration and audit trails; changes nothing.

Access levels

One scale of letters is used for every kind of resource. Some levels include others ("implies"), and a cell always lists every level it holds, so a reader sees exactly what is granted.

LevelNameIncludesMeaning
NNoneNo access. The default for every cell.
RReadSee the resource, change nothing.
XRead and exportRRead, and take a copy out of the platform through Database Management. Every export is logged.
CCreateRAdd new records; never change existing ones. The level used for appending to regulated data and audit trails.
UUpdateC, RCreate and change records within the group's constraint. Removing a configuration record is an update to "retired", never a delete. Never held by a person on regulated or history data.
AApproveRApprove or release another person's work. In this version an approval is an attributable, time-stamped record, not a 21 CFR Part 11 electronic signature.
OOperateRStart, stop or trigger a run; no change to its definition.
KConfigureAdminister a tool or accounts. Held only by admin. On accounts it means reading and changing account records, which are personal data.
DDeleteRemove platform components on the host. Never data. Held only by admin, on platform administration.

Data classes

Each resource group has one class, and the invariants are written against the classes.

  • Regulated data: records produced while making product, such as runs, telemetry, persisted controller state and run logs. Created once and never changed or deleted by anyone; corrections are new records.
  • Audit history: append-only trails of who did what, including approvals and export logs. Written only by database functions and triggers.
  • Personal data: accounts, names, e-mail addresses, unit assignments and access decisions.
  • Configuration: master data, recipes, controllers, schedules, settings, dashboards and tools, changed under the group's approval rule.

Constraints

A constraint narrows a level in a cell. A person passes when any of their roles holds the level without a constraint, or with a constraint that holds.

ConstraintWhere it appliesRule
own_unitoperator reading telemetry, runs and run logsOnly the units assigned to the person, including every zone of those units and zones added later.
assigned_runoperator executing or stopping runsOnly a run another person created while holding production_manager (or a schedule such a person created), in one of the operator's units.
assign_onlyproduction_manager on recipesAssign approved recipes and approved parameter sets to units; never edit them.
draft_onlyengineer on recipes and controllersEdit drafts only. Once approved, a definition is frozen and a change starts a new draft.
existing_slotmaintenance on devices and onboardingRe-onboard a board into a slot that already exists; creating a new slot is refused.
commissioning_unitengineer publishing on command topicsCommand only a unit flagged for commissioning and with no active run.
not_own_authorevery Approve (A) cellApprove only another person's work. Compares persons, not accounts.
qa_dual_controladmin on accounts and unit assignmentsGrants wait for a qa person; removing access acts at once.

Invariants

Invariants are rules the policy itself must satisfy. The matrix rules are checked on every compile and by python3 apps/iam/compiler/cli.py check. The workflow rules are checked when a change is approved: I17 by the User Manager, I8 by the planned Policy UI. The database rules (I9, I10, I15) are checked by the database deploy, which rolls back if the live grants differ from the policy.

CodeRule
I1No role holds U or D on regulated or history data.
I2admin holds nothing but K on regulated, history or personal data, including through tools.
I3auditor holds only R or X.
I4On a group with an approval rule, no role holds both (C, U or O) and A.
I5The two scientist roles hold nothing on runs, schedules, MQTT topics and controller state, and at most Read on telemetry (never export or write; Read by decision, IAM 3.2b).
I6Production roles hold nothing on the AI workbench; engineer at most R.
I7qp holds no C, U or O anywhere, and holds A on runs.
I8A policy version is applied only after approval by someone other than the submitter, whose own role it does not widen.
I9Nothing in the platform's schemas is reachable without a verified identity.
I10Each service's grants stay within its ceiling; no service approves on its own or rewrites regulated or history tables unless a waiver covers it.
I11A tool cannot widen a role's access to the data it reaches, unless a waiver covers it.
I12At least one role other than admin holds A on the policy and on accounts, and at least one of those roles makes no changes there and is in use; admin never does.
I13Only admin holds K or D; D only on platform administration.
I14, I16Every cell compiles to something real, and cells list every level they imply.
I15The privileges in the database equal what the policy compiles to, and every table belongs to a group.
I17No person holds an admin account and a qa account at the same time.

Two waivers are accepted and stated in the policy with their compensating controls and a review date of 2027-10-27. W1: the Node-RED editor runs with the ingest account, which must insert telemetry. Its controls: the flows are deployed from the repository, the health check compares the running flows with the repository, the editor admits only the roles the policy gives Node-RED flows (at the sign-in and inside the editor), and every deploy in the editor is logged with the person's name. W2: a learning controller updates its Q-table during a run; every update is also appended as an event with the run id.

The Access Policy shows the applied policy and its history, and is where a qa person confirms a bootstrap or rollback version (slice 4.3). Since slice 4.4 an admin drafts a change there and a qa person who is none of its authors approves it, and the host operator proposes a git skeleton change for the same approval (Changing the access policy). Applying an approved version is slice 4.5 and not built: nothing approved changes anyone's access yet. Version 1 exists since slice 4.2a, and every deploy refuses a git change that gives access (the skeleton gate), break-glass included, whether or not a version proposes it, so until approvals can be applied no change that widens access can deploy; a narrowing change in git is accepted at the next deploy. python3 apps/iam/compiler/cli.py check runs the invariants.

How the policy is enforced, in layers

No single check is trusted alone. A request passes five layers, each compiled from the same policy; a message to the broker passes its own, listed last.

  1. Sign-in gate per host. Every web UI signs in through Keycloak. Each gated host admits only the roles that hold some level on a group served there. A signed-in person without such a role sees a "No access" page naming the roles that may open it. For example the policy admits auditor, qa and qp to Database Management, and admin, qa, qp and auditor to the User Manager. python3 apps/iam/compiler/cli.py hosts lists who each host admits. Grafana signs people in itself; its own role setting is compiled from the same policy: engineer is Editor, the other roles holding Read on dashboards are Viewer, and every other role is refused. Grafana Admin is never given through the sign-in. Node-RED's editor signs people in a second time and gives the rights compiled from the policy: engineer may change and deploy flows but not install palette modules, and no other role has any right in it. The AI workbench (JupyterHub) likewise admits exactly the roles the policy admits to its host (admin, bio_scientist, control_scientist, engineer, qa); admin, the only role holding Configure there, is hub administrator without the right to open anyone's workspace (through the hub role workbench-admin; until the fix of 31 October 2026 the platform did not meet this, see the known gaps), and removing a person from the hub keeps their home folder. The device onboarding wizard admits only engineer and maintenance, the roles that may register boards, and checks again at every renewal of the sign-in during a run, so a board is not erased for someone who lost the role. pgAdmin admits only admin, checked at sign-in.
  2. Verified token in every service. The six Python services (scheduler, Monitor, Database Management, the Config UI's platform API, the User Manager and, since IAM 3.5, iam-api, which issues the MQTT Explorer's credentials) check every request against the compiled route table. They trust only a signed access token verified against Keycloak's public keys, never identity headers that anything inside the cluster could send. Each route belongs to one group and needs one level; a route missing from the table is refused.
  3. Network policies. Each of the eight application services (scheduler, Monitor, Database Management, the Config UI, its database API, the User Manager, Node-RED and iam-api, which only the MQTT Explorer's sign-in proxy reaches) accepts connections only from its listed callers, so another program in the cluster or a forged request cannot reach it at all. Since IAM 3.2b the database API (config-api) also accepts the AI workbench's notebooks, which reach nothing else of the platform but Keycloak, and only while IAM_POSTGREST_JWT and IAM_DB_ROLES are true: each request carries the person's own sign-in, and the database applies that person's role and row rules. Both sides of that opening are compiled from the access policy. The portal, MQTT Explorer's page, the message broker, Grafana and the workbench's own hub are not covered.
  4. Database roles and row-level security. While IAM_DB_ROLES is true, a person's requests through the Config UI's database API run as that person's own database role. Each service logs in as its own role. Row-level security (a filter the database applies to every query) limits an operator to the telemetry and runs of their units. Triggers refuse edits to approved definitions and to append-only records. This layer holds even if an application has a bug.
  5. Approvals in the database. Approval functions check the approver's role and that the approver is not an author, using the person from the verified token. A service cannot approve on its own.
  6. Message broker. Every broker client authenticates. Boards and the platform's services use the LAN port; with IAM_MQTT_PERSON=true people use only their own short-lived credential from the MQTT Explorer, accepted only on the WebSocket listener, carrying the topics their role's cells give. A send right exists only for a unit flagged for commissioning without a running run, and the broker's credential sync re-derives it every 15 seconds from the database.

Some constraints are checked only in one layer. assigned_run is checked only by the database's run functions, and own_unit by row-level security and by the Monitor and scheduler reads themselves.

Report-only and enforce

The services can run in two modes, set by IAM_ENFORCE in config.env.

  • Report-only (IAM_ENFORCE=false, the state in which IAM 2.6 was deployed): a request the route table refuses is let through, and the service writes medcea_iam: would refuse … to its log. In the same way the scheduler logs run_logs: would withhold when it shows a run's log to a role that will not see it under enforcement.
  • Enforce (IAM_ENFORCE=true): the service answers 401 (no token or a bad one), 403 (route or role not allowed) or 503 (the service cannot check, for example the route table or keys are missing).

The services enforce since 31 October 2026, 09:54 UTC (IAM_ENFORCE=true; the policy history holds the enforcement_enabled event). Two places always enforce, whatever IAM_ENFORCE says: Database Management (exports) and the User Manager's administration port. The database layer has its own switch, IAM_DB_ROLES, which has been true since 30 October 2026, and the operator unit filter in the Monitor and scheduler applies whenever either switch is true. Only while both are false do those two services log own_unit: would limit … instead of filtering.

The administrator turns enforcement on with ./medcea.sh: area "IAM switches (enable / roll back)", the IAM_ENFORCE action, then enable. medcea.sh first lists its preconditions as a checklist the administrator confirms: IAM_DB_ROLES is true, the report-only trial is over, and every operator has a unit in effect. It then takes the deploy lock, runs python3 tests/iam-routes-diff.py --strict, sets the switch in config.env and runs ./deploy-infra.sh, stopping at the first failure. Services read the new value within about a minute without a restart. Rollback sets it back to false and runs ./deploy-infra.sh again.

Every transition of IAM_ENFORCE or IAM_DB_ROLES appends an enforcement_enabled or enforcement_disabled event, naming the switch, to the tamper-evident policy history. ./health-check.sh (check iamenforce) fails when the value the services read differs from config.env, when IAM_ENFORCE is true while IAM_DB_ROLES is false, or when a service's own fallback copy is still false under true. It warns while IAM_ENFORCE is false.

Dual control: the maker is never the checker

Every approval needs two different persons. The platform compares the person_id carried in each verified token, not account names, so one person with two accounts is still one person. person_id is set to the account's own id when it is first enabled; changing it is itself a decision that waits for qa.

An approval function refuses when the approver is the author, submitter, creator or executor of the record, or, for an account decision, its subject; and when the change would widen the approver's own role. For account decisions the accounts are compared as well.

Rule I17 keeps the administrator and the independent approver apart: no person may hold an admin and a qa account at the same time. The User Manager checks this against Keycloak when a role or person_id change is proposed and again when it is confirmed.

Account decisions

Every change an administrator makes to an account in the User Manager is recorded as an account decision. What happens next depends on whether the change gives access or takes it away.

ChangeEffect
Grant (an approved access request)Waits for qa. The request reads "approved", but the account stays disabled with no role until confirmed.
Activation of an accountWaits for qa, because an enabled account gets back everything its role gives (and, while IAM_GATES is false, the AI workbench even without a role).
Role change that adds any (group, level) the old role did not haveWaits for qa.
New unit assignmentWaits for qa (see Unit assignments).
person_id changeAlways waits for qa.
E-mail settings changeWaits for qa.
DeactivationActs at once, signs the person out and revokes their MQTT credentials; reviewed by qa afterwards.
Role change that only narrowsActs at once, revokes MQTT credentials; reviewed afterwards. A widening role change revokes them when qa confirms it.
Removal of a unitActs at once; reviewed afterwards.

An account has at most one open decision at a time. A deactivation is the exception: it withdraws the account's waiting decisions. An administrator may withdraw a waiting decision in the User Manager; a unit assignment is withdrawn in the account's Units section (or with units.sh remove on the host). The last enabled admin and the last enabled qa cannot be removed.

Confirming, refusing and reviewing

  1. Sign in to the User Manager as a qa person and open the Decisions tab.
  2. "Waiting for qa" lists the decisions to confirm or refuse; "To review" lists the changes that already acted; "All" lists every decision.
  3. Open a decision and read what it will do. For a waiting decision choose Confirm or Refuse; a note is optional to confirm and required to refuse. For an applied one choose Mark reviewed. Confirming applies the change in Keycloak in the same step. Refusing a grant deletes the requested account, so the person can apply again. If you cannot check a decision, for example because you made it or it concerns your own account, the page says why.

A red banner at the top of the Decisions tab ("Keycloak differs from the decisions") lists any account whose live role or state is not explained by a recorded decision, for example a role granted directly in the Keycloak console.

Each decision row keeps the maker, the subject, the change, the reason, and the checker with time and note. Once checked the row is final: a database trigger lets only the check columns be filled, once. Confirmations, refusals, reviews and withdrawals are also appended to the hash-chained policy history. Status and role changes are kept in the append-only account status history.

./health-check.sh (check iamdecisions) warns when a decision has waited more than 7 days, or when an e-mail settings change is pending.

Unit assignments

Operators are assigned units, not zones. An operator with no unit in effect sees no telemetry and no runs and can start none. Since 12 November 2026 an admin assigns and removes units in the User Manager, in the Units section of the account (see User Manager). The administrator is recorded as the maker from their own sign-in.

An assignment is only proposed: nothing takes effect until a qa person who is neither the maker nor the subject confirms it in the Decisions tab. A refusal applies nothing. A removal acts at once, and removing a waiting assignment withdraws it. The User Manager refuses to assign a unit to an account that is disabled, is not an operator or has no person_id; removing is always allowed. Only admin reads or changes an account's units; qa and auditor see every unit decision in the Decisions tab.

On the platform host apps/iam/units.sh does the same, under the deploy lock:

./apps/iam/units.sh list
./apps/iam/units.sh assign <username> UNIT01 --by <your username>
./apps/iam/units.sh remove <username> UNIT01 --by <your username>

--by names the person running the command, who is recorded as the maker. The script cannot prove who ran it, since whoever runs it controls the host. So every assignment made by units.sh can be confirmed only after the qa person ticks the box "I did not run units.sh for this assignment." The attestation is stored with the confirmation note. An assignment made in the User Manager needs no attestation: its maker comes from a verified sign-in.

--bootstrap (host only) applies an assignment at once, before any check, and is allowed only while no other enabled qa account could confirm it. The decision still waits for qa; the User Manager marks it "in effect before the check", and a refusal removes the unit.

Every unit that takes effect or is removed appends unit_assigned or unit_removed to the hash-chained policy history, with the qa person as actor for a confirmed assignment.

The quarterly access review

The Access review tab of the User Manager holds one review per quarter. A qa person creates it and signs it off; auditor and qp can read it.

  1. Open Access review and choose "Create this quarter's review". The snapshot is taken at that moment and never changes.
  2. Read the snapshot: every account with its role, state, person_id and last login; the units; anything unexplained at the time of the review; decisions waiting for qa; decisions since the last review; the waivers; the IAM switches; and the policy version and hash-chain verdict.
  3. Add an optional note and choose "Sign off" followed by the quarter. Signing off cannot be undone.

Signing off a review that lists unexplained roles accepts them: the drift banner in the Decisions tab stops showing them until a later change to that account. It does not accept the unrecorded accounts it lists (enabled accounts that no request, decision or status change names and that ./deploy-infra.sh did not seed): by the owner's decision of 9 November 2026 only seeded accounts are exempt, so such an account counts as drift, in the banner and in the health check's Account drift, until it is recorded (an access request and its decision) or removed. The acceptance of an unexplained role lasts only while that review is the latest signed off: the next review's snapshot no longer lists the role, so after its sign-off the role is unexplained again and must be explained by a decision.

Approvals of configuration

Groups with an approval rule are either blocking (nothing is used until approved) or review (qa confirms after the fact).

WhatRuleWho approves
RecipesBlocking. Status draft, approved or retired. While IAM_DB_ROLES is true, the database refuses to assign a recipe that is not approved (in the Configuration UI's Recipe ↔ Unit Permissions) or to run one, and an approved recipe cannot be edited; while it is false these are warnings.qa
Control algorithms and parameter setsBlocking. A run uses only approved algorithms and approved parameter sets.qa
Scheduler settings (log retention)Blocking. A new value waits as a pending change and applies only after a qa person other than its author confirms it. While one waits, only its proposer may replace it; anyone else's new proposal for that setting is refused until qa approves or returns it or its proposer withdraws it. The database also enforces minimums (compress after at least 1 day).qa
Unit commissioning flag (test mode)Blocking to turn on: an engineer proposes it with a reason in the Units tab, and it takes effect only after a qa person other than the proposer approves it, because it opens MQTT command rights to the unit. It is refused while the unit has a run running or scheduled, at the proposal and again at the approval, and no run can be scheduled or start on a flagged unit. Turning it off is a narrowing: it applies at once and qa reviews it afterwards. qa may return a waiting proposal with a reason, and its proposer may withdraw it.qa
Master data and devicesReview. Each change may be confirmed after the fact; an unconfirmed one blocks nothing. These reviews are not listed in the Approvals tab (a known gap).qa
Persisted controller state (Q-tables)Blocking. Retiring is an approved, recorded event; the next run starts cold.qa
Run releaseRelease of a completed run, in the Configuration UI's Approvals tab, by a person who neither created, changed nor executed it (any attempt), with an optional note. Refused while a change to the run has no attributed person, when no recorded person created or started it (a run from before attribution), and for a run that is not completed or already released. There is no hold or refusal: a run that is not released stays unreleased. A released run cannot be set back for a retry.qp

Editing an approved recipe, algorithm or parameter set is refused while IAM_DB_ROLES is true; a change starts a new draft. An approval is also refused while the record carries a change with no attributed person since its last approval.

To retire a Q-table, a qa person opens the Control Models tab of the Config UI, finds the unit in the Production Units table, chooses Retire… next to the algorithm under Learned State and gives a reason, which is recorded. Nothing is deleted.

Each approval writes a row to medcea.approval with the record, a hash of its content, the persons who authored it, and the approver's account, person, name, role and source. Returning a draft or a proposal (action return, with the reason), withdrawing a proposal (action withdraw) and reviewing a change that applied at once (action review) are rows there too; no approval rule counts a return or a withdrawal as an approval. A commissioning proposal is a row in medcea.pending_change (proposer account, person, name, role, source, reason, time, and when it applied at once); the flag change itself is in medcea.row_change, on the unit's updated_by_* columns and in the tamper-evident policy history. A retired Q-table keeps its full state, and each of its channels gains an approval row with action retire and the reason. A release is a row in medcea.run_release (one per run) and an approval row with action release, both with the note.

Attribution: who did what

The 14 attributed tables (master data, devices, recipes, controllers, runs, schedules and others) carry created_by and updated_by fields: account, person, name, role and source. A database trigger fills them from the verified actor of the transaction and overwrites whatever a client sends. A service acting for a person records that person, with source person via followed by the service's database login; a schedule firing acts as system:scheduler on behalf of the person who created the schedule.

Every change to those tables is also appended to medcea.row_change. The approval functions read it to decide who counts as an author.

The tamper-evident policy history

iam_policy.history is a hash chain: each event stores the hash of the previous one, so a changed or removed event breaks every hash after it. Triggers refuse UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE on it for every role, the owner included. It records:

  • enforcement_enabled and enforcement_disabled, with the switch (IAM_DB_ROLES, IAM_ENFORCE or IAM_MQTT_PERSON);
  • mqtt_credential_issued: every MQTT Explorer credential, with its user name, the person, their role, the topics and the expiry (never the password);
  • unit_assigned and unit_removed;
  • account_decision_confirmed, _refused, _reviewed and _withdrawn;
  • mqtt_credentials_retired: MQTT Explorer credentials ended by ./deploy-infra.sh because the MQTT policy or the IAM_MQTT_PERSON switch changed, with the number and the reason;
  • commissioning_enabled and commissioning_disabled: a unit's commissioning flag turned on (by the qa person who approved it) or off (by the engineer, at once), with the unit, the proposal, the proposer and the reason;
  • break_glass_seen: ./deploy-infra.sh found Node-RED running without its own sign-in (NR_ADMIN_AUTH=off) and turned it on again, with the time Node-RED started that way;
  • since IAM 4.2a, the access policy's own versions: skeleton_accepted (with the skeleton it replaced) and skeleton_synced, draft_created, status_changed, apply_started and bootstrap_applied (version 1, with the person who claimed it, the git commit and the digest of every compiled output);
  • account_seeded: an account ./deploy-infra.sh created or gave a person_id, and, once, the qa, engineer and (since 10 November 2026) platform admin accounts of the install as they were found (observed); username, account id, role and person_id only;
  • break_glass_seen with source: file and break_glass_ended: a deploy compiled a policy file of its own (see policy break-glass), with the file's SHA-256 and the reason, and its end per component;
  • older zone_assigned and zone_removed events from before units replaced zones.

./health-check.sh runs iam_policy.verify_chain() (check iamchain) and reports "hash chain intact, N event(s)" or the first broken event.

Known limit: the chain catches any edit that does not rebuild it. It does not catch a database superuser who disables the triggers, drops the newest events or re-hashes the chain from an edited event onward. That needs the head of the chain anchored outside the database, which is not built.

Exports and the export log

Database Management lets a person holding X take a copy of tables and views of schema medcea, covering exactly the groups where their role holds X. An object outside those groups refuses the whole export and nothing is logged. A file saved on the platform goes to apps/database/exports/ and never overwrites an existing file.

Each export writes one row to iam_policy.export_log naming who exported which groups and objects (with row counts) and when, before the file is produced. The file header carries the export number; the page shows the export number and the start of the file's SHA-256, and the service log records the full hash. The export log is append-only for every role.

What is never deleted

  • Audit histories: the policy history, export log, approvals, row changes, account status history, access request history and the User Manager's change log are append-only: database triggers refuse changing or deleting their rows for every role, the owner included.
  • Device placement history: every placement, move and removal of a board.
  • Run logs: kept for good. The scheduler's own job sys_log_retention (daily at 03:15 UTC) compresses the log of a finished run after log_compress_days. It never deletes one, and no person can delete or compress logs. log_delete_days remains a setting but nothing reads it.
  • Q-tables: retired, never deleted.
  • Configuration: recipes, schedules and similar records are retired, not deleted. No person holds a DELETE grant on data.

While IAM_ENFORCE is true, a run's log is shown only to roles that hold Read on run logs; maintenance, qc and qp see the run without its log.

Accounts on this install are test accounts

This install is a research prototype run by one person. Every platform account on it is a test account used by that person to exercise a role; none belongs to cultivation, quality or audit staff. Read every record that names these accounts with that in mind: a maker and a checker shown as different accounts can be the same human.

The platform was installed afresh on 11 November 2026 from release v0.5.0 (exercise E28). The evidence this chapter cites with an earlier date (decision, approval, pending-change and history event numbers, health check results, hub logs) is that of the previous install, which ran from October 2026 (upgraded in place to v0.4.0 on 1 November) until 11 November 2026. The new install started with an empty database and a new Keycloak realm, so its records are numbered from 1 again and a number cited here may name an unrelated record there. The previous install's records survive only in its backups: 20261111-194018Z, taken just before the reinstall, in BACKUP_DIR until the nightly run deletes it after BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS, unless copied off the host (see Backup and restore).

The current install (since 11 November 2026). Its accounts are the three made by the install. Its IAM switches start with IAM_GATES, IAM_NETPOL and IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES on; version 1 is applied and waits for a qa confirmation, which the platform refuses until Bring IAM to full enforcement has run.

Holds engineer since decision 17 ("for testing", qa to engineer, confirmed by svieira, during the onboarding exercises), so it was not the approver of Superset stage C as planned (N6): svieira approved versions 15 and 16 (owner decision of 8 November 2026).
sergio_qpqpenabledTest account of the same person, created on 7 November 2026 for exercise E27 as Superset's viewer (the plan called it test-qp): created by the owner, approved by admin, confirmed by svieira.
developeroperatordisabledDemo account made by older installs. Deactivated on 31 October 2026 as a test of the retire path: its units were removed with units.sh, then the account was deactivated in the User Manager (decision 12).

New installs no longer create the developer and viewer demo accounts (IAM 3.1). Before real staff use the platform, give each person their own account through Request access, and deactivate the test accounts in the User Manager.

Known gaps and single-person controls

  • Zone moves. Telemetry is filtered by the zone's current unit. Moving a zone to another unit, which engineer may do, gives that unit's operators the zone's whole history without an account decision. It is recorded only in medcea.row_change. Deferred.
  • Open AI workbench sessions. The workbench checks a person's role at each sign-in, not continuously. After a role removal or a deactivation, a workbench session and an open notebook keep working until the sign-in runs again, at the latest after 5 minutes (an open notebook tab after about 10 minutes; until 1 November 2026, an hour). Personal API tokens a person created on the hub keep working until the administrator removes that person from the hub (which keeps their files). Notebooks run code; of the platform's services they reach only Keycloak and the database API, with the person's own sign-in, for reads only, which follows a role change or a deactivation within five minutes (IAM 3.2b).
  • Fixed 31 October 2026: the workbench administrator could open workspaces. Until then a hub administrator held JupyterHub's built-in administrator role, which includes creating a token in any person's name and opening their workspace. The setting the platform relied on to prevent it (admin_access: false) has done nothing since JupyterHub 2.0, and the health check trusted it. The live test tests/iam-workbench.sh found it on 31 October 2026 (step W4: the hub created a token for the test scientist, and the scientist's workspace accepted it; step W3 passed only because the test did not press "Authorize" on the page the hub showed). The fix gives administrators the narrower hub role workbench-admin and nobody the built-in role, and the test now requires the hub to refuse (403) both the token and the authorize step. The database showed no token created by an administrator for another person; deploying the fix removes the built-in role from the accounts that held it (admin and two earlier test administrators).
  • Node-RED editor tokens in the sign-in proxy's log. Node-RED's sign-in returns the editor token in the address it redirects to, and Node-RED's sign-in proxy logs each request's full address, so every editor sign-in since the Phase 3 deploy left its token in that proxy's log (found 31 October 2026). Someone who can read that log and also passes the engineer gate could use another engineer's editor session until it expires, and Node-RED's audit log would name the other engineer. The 8 hours the platform had set were never in effect (Node-RED ignored the setting where it stood), so a session lasted Node-RED's default of a week; since 1 November 2026 it lasts one hour, and the deploy of that day ended every longer one. Fixed the same day: the proxy no longer logs requests to /, the path that carries the token (exclude_logging_paths), and the logged sessions were ended by clearing Node-RED's session file. Editor sessions survive a Node-RED restart (they are kept on its volume), so ending them takes clearing /data/.sessions.json; see troubleshooting.
  • Telemetry can leave through a notebook. A scientist holds Read on telemetry, not export, but a notebook runs the person's code with internet access (package installs, GitHub). When a notebook is committed to git its outputs are removed automatically (nbstripout, set up in every workspace at each start), and a check behind the filter refuses a commit whose notebooks still hold outputs, also when a repository's own settings turn the filter off or it could not be installed; a person who deliberately skips git's checks (git commit --no-verify) with the filter off is not stopped. Code and text cells, other files in the repository, downloads from the browser and anything a person's code sends elsewhere are not checked. What is read is attributable (each request runs as the person); what leaves afterwards is not recorded. Mitigated by the instructions in the workspace and the manual.
  • Workbench home folders: one nightly copy on the same host (until 1 November 2026, none). They are kept when a workspace stops, when a person is removed from the hub or loses the workbench, and across every workbench redeploy. Since 1 November 2026 the nightly backup copies them (see the next item); before, nothing copied them anywhere. Deleting the namespace or MicroK8s (--uninstall-infra, --uninstall-all, ./deploy-infra.sh --reset or --uninstall, or a yes to "Fully wipe MicroK8s and reinstall?") deletes them; those commands list them, with the newest backup, and say how to keep them before they ask. The research repository stays the copy of record for notebooks.
  • Backups on the same host (1 November 2026). The nightly backup (Backup and restore) writes to BACKUP_DIR on the platform host itself, by default on the same disk as the data. A disk failure, a lost or stolen machine, or anyone with the host's administrator rights can therefore take both the data and its backups; the deploy warns when they share a disk. Until BACKUP_DIR is on another disk, or the folders are copied off the host, it protects against mistakes, a failed upgrade and a reinstall, not against losing the machine. The backups are not encrypted (mode 700 for the deploying account only) and hold Keycloak's password hashes and client secrets and people's git tokens. A restore is a manual procedure and writes nothing into the platform's records. No restore has been tested on production yet (exercise E12).
  • Onboarding into a new slot by maintenance. The onboarding wizard admits maintenance, which may only re-onboard into a slot that already exists, but the wizard does not check this itself. If a maintenance person chooses an empty slot, the board is erased and flashed before the database refuses the registration, and the board is left unregistered. No account on this install holds maintenance today.
  • Test messages sent from the host (6 November 2026). Send test message and flash-device.sh --send-test connect with the board's own credential, read from its provisioning record on the host, so the broker and the database cannot tell such a message from the board's own: only its content says so ("sent_from": "host", source). Whoever has a shell on the platform host can read those records and send as any board, within its slot's topics; the wizard's log names the person only for messages sent from the wizard. This is the host operator's existing reach (the records already hold every board's password in plain text), not a new one.
  • Board credentials on the board itself. Since 5 November 2026 a board talks to the broker over TLS only, so its MQTT password no longer crosses the network in clear. On the board, though, the WiFi passphrase and the MQTT password are stored unencrypted in its flash: anyone holding a board can read them over USB and then publish as that board within its own slot's topics. WebREPL also stays on (port 8266, a nine-character password per board; nine is the most WebREPL accepts): anyone on the network who has or guesses it gets a Python prompt on the board. ESP32 flash encryption and a firmware without WebREPL would close both; neither is built. Treat a lost board as a lost credential and mark it Inactive.
  • Onboarding from the host shell without a platform identity. Whoever has a shell on the platform host and serial port access can flash a board without signing in: flash-device.sh --unregistered, declining the sign-in when a terminal run offers to continue unregistered, continuing when the slots cannot be read, and --ui-insecure. None of these registers the board or gives it a credential. They stay as the host operator's break-glass path (see the decision record).
  • Node-RED flows outside the repository. A flow built in the editor is reported by the health check as a warning, not blocked. Code in a flow runs inside Node-RED and can read what Node-RED holds: the ingest database password, the broker account, Node-RED's sign-in secret and the deploy scripts' token. An engineer who means to can therefore get round the rule that palette modules come only from the repository. The audit log and the health check make such use visible; they do not prevent it.
  • Open Grafana sessions. Grafana checks a person's role only at sign-in. A deactivation or a role removal does not end a Grafana session that is already open: the person keeps their Grafana role, and with it every unit's telemetry, until the session ends, 5 minutes after it was last used and at the latest one hour after its sign-in; the next sign-in checks the role again (a deactivated account cannot sign in). Until 1 November 2026 it was one hour whether used or not. A change to who gets which Grafana role (the access policy) reaches open sessions the same way: Grafana keeps its sessions across the restart that change causes, since it keeps its database (decision record, "Grafana keeps its data"); until then that restart ended every session at once.
  • Editors' own Grafana dashboards are not reviewed, and can be restored only whole (1 November 2026). A Grafana Editor (engineer) may create dashboards, or "Save as" copies of the platform's, and Grafana keeps them, with folders, annotations and alert rules, until an Editor deletes them. They are not in the repository, no second person reviews them, and Grafana records only who saved one last, in its own database. Since 1 November 2026 the nightly backup copies that database, but an administrator can put it back only whole, to the state of a night; a reinstall deletes it (after a warning that names it). They read through Grafana's own database account like every dashboard, so they show nothing a Viewer could not query anyway. The platform's own dashboards stay read-only and change only through the repository.
  • Sign out and switching accounts in one browser (1 November 2026). Sign out ends, at once, the sign-in gate of the app it is chosen in, the platform sign-in and the AI Workbench's own session. The other apps keep their own sessions for a short while, so after a sign-out, or when another person signs in on the same browser, an app can still show the previous person:
    • the sign-in gates of the other hosts: up to 4 minutes;
    • the AI Workbench hub: up to 5 minutes; an open JupyterLab tab: about 10 minutes, though never another person's workspace;
    • Grafana: up to 5 minutes after its last use, and up to one hour after its sign-in while a tab keeps it in use (a dashboard with auto-refresh does);
    • the Node-RED editor: up to one hour after it was opened, still acting, and logged, as the previous person (sessions issued before 1 November 2026 lasted a week; Node-RED drops every stored session longer than the hour at each start, so the deploy of that day ended them);
    • Superset (installed since 8 November 2026): up to 5 minutes after its last use, and up to one hour after its sign-in while it is in use; its own Logout ends the platform sign-in and the AI Workbench's and portal's sessions too;
    • pgAdmin: up to 60 minutes without use, at most one day in use. pgAdmin does not follow the platform sign-in at all: it is bound only by those limits, its own Logout and a restart. A shorter session is not possible: pgAdmin's start-up passes the session length in days to its web server as a whole number of seconds, and a fraction of a day stopped pgAdmin from starting (1 November 2026).
    Live connections already open stay connected until their tab is closed: JupyterLab kernels, MQTT Explorer's broker connection (with the person's own credential until it expires or is revoked) and Grafana's live updates. If the AI Workbench does not answer, Sign out stops on its error page after the platform sign-in has ended; the workbench's own session then ends within its 5 minutes and the portal's gate within 4. The portal's own Sign Out buttons still end only the portal's gate session. The manual tells people on a shared computer not to tick Remember me, to sign out and close the browser, and to use pgAdmin's own Logout.
  • Superset dashboards are published without review (Superset stage C, decision N11). Since Superset was installed (8 November 2026), a builder can publish a dashboard, and every viewer whose datasets use the MedCEA connection sees it; no second person reviews it first, and it is not in the repository (importing dashboards from the repository is deferred, N9). Like Grafana, Superset reads every unit's telemetry through its own database account (svc_superset: master data and measurements, read only, no runs), so its viewers and builders see every unit.
  • Grafana reads every unit. Grafana is gated by role since Phase 3.1, but its dashboards read telemetry of every unit through Grafana's own database account, which is why operator has no Grafana. A Viewer can send Grafana any query that account may run (master data, measurements and runs); hiding Explore from Viewers is not a boundary.
  • Grafana's local admin. One break-glass account holds Grafana Admin, with its own generated password in config.env and the credentials file. Whoever operates the host can read it; its use is logged only by Grafana.
  • Shared MQTT Explorer account (closed 31 October 2026). Until IAM_MQTT_PERSON was turned on, MQTT Explorer connected with one shared account that read and wrote every topic, also on the LAN port, so commands sent from it named no person. Since then each person gets a short-lived credential of their own, accepted only on the WebSocket listener, and the broker refuses the shared account on both ports (tests/iam-mqtt.sh M5). Since 1 November 2026 the shared account no longer exists: a rollback of the switch leaves the Explorer without a credential instead of bringing it back.
  • MQTT Explorer credentials outlive a sign-out. Signing out of the platform does not end a credential; it ends after at most 8 hours. Deactivation, a role change, clearing a unit's commissioning flag and a run start take effect at the broker's next check, within about 15 seconds; a connection already open stays open, but each message is checked. If the broker cannot read the credentials from the database, it stops accepting changes to them for at most 30 seconds and then admits no person credential until it can read them again.
  • The broker's WebSocket listener is reachable inside the cluster. No network policy covers the broker yet, so a program in the cluster that holds a leaked Explorer credential could use it directly, not only through the Explorer's sign-in, until the credential expires. Deferred (see the decision record).
  • Approval and commissioning screens (closed 31 October 2026). Until then qa could approve drafts and pending changes only through the database functions, and nothing in the Configuration UI flagged a unit for commissioning, so an engineer's MQTT Explorer could only read. The Approvals tab and the Units tab's Commissioning column now do both (see commissioning a unit); a walk-through on production the same evening used both (see the decision record).
  • Fixed 31 October 2026: the Configuration UI's deploy failed. The page had grown to 254 KB, and kubectl apply keeps a copy of the whole ConfigMap in an annotation that holds at most 256 KiB, so the frontend deploy stopped with "metadata.annotations: Too long" and the old page kept running. Found at the deploy of the approval screens. The deploy now replaces or creates that ConfigMap instead of applying it, as the scheduler deploy already did (commit 15e8d0b); see troubleshooting.
  • Fixed 31 October 2026: the MQTT Explorer sent wildcard topics. In the walk-through the engineer copied the pattern from Your rights (medcea/+/+/control/#) into the topic box. Sending to a topic with + or # is a protocol error, so the broker closed the connection and the page showed "Reconnecting…"; nothing was delivered. The page now refuses such a topic before sending and names an example, and the rights note says its topics are patterns (commit a294b06).
  • pgAdmin's secrets in plain text (closed 1 November 2026). Until then pgAdmin's sign-in client secret and its first-start password (the platform administrator's) were plain values in the pgAdmin deployment, readable by anyone allowed to read deployments in the cluster. They are now in a Kubernetes Secret, pgAdmin's deployment keeps no older copies (ReplicaSets) that still hold them, and the health check (pgadminroles) fails while the deployment or such a copy still carries them as plain values. On the install of that date the client secret is to be regenerated once in Keycloak after the deploy, since it was readable until then; an install made after that date never had it in plain text and needs no regeneration.
  • Run release screen (closed 31 October 2026). Until then the database could record a release, but no screen called it, so qp could not release a completed run from the platform. The Approvals tab now lists the completed, unreleased runs for qp and releases them (see releasing a completed run); the Scheduler shows a Released badge. No account on this install holds qp (since the reinstall of 11 November 2026; on the previous install the test account sergio_qp held it from 7 November), and no release has been made live yet (exercise E6): make a qp account through Request access first.
  • No hold, deviation or CAPA record for a run. qp can release a completed run or leave it unreleased; the platform records no hold, refusal or deviation, and nothing says why a run stays unreleased. Deviations and CAPA (Spec RACI 10) are not built. Decided 31 October 2026.
  • Runs completed before attribution cannot be released. A run completed before migration 008b is recorded as created by migration:008, with no person and no change history, so the platform cannot tell who created or executed it. Such a run is listed for qp with the reason "no recorded person created or started this run" and the database refuses to release it, because the rule that the releaser neither created nor executed the run cannot be checked. These runs stay unreleased in the queue, and they are not counted on the tab. They are never released: decided by the platform owner on 1 November 2026 (see the decision record).
  • After-the-fact reviews of master data and devices are not in the Approvals tab. qa can review them only through the database function; an unreviewed change blocks nothing.
  • A few minutes of a differing route-table digest (IAM 4.2a). Between the database deploy and ./deploy-infra.sh of slice 4.2a the database and the route table disagree about the route table's digest, for minutes. No refusal by the User Manager follows from it; iamenforce and tests/iam-schema.sh are red until ./deploy-infra.sh has run.
  • The host policy file's digests are not keyed (IAM 4.2a). The account that deploys the platform can rewrite state/policy-applied.yaml with hand-recomputed digests. The health check finds it (it compares the whole body with the database) and the next deploy overwrites it; the onboarding wizard and flash-device.sh compile it as it is in between.
  • A queued account fact is not read again from Keycloak (IAM 4.2a). A fact that waited in state/seed-facts.jsonl is recorded as it was written. It grants nothing (who may approve is read from Keycloak at the time), and it cannot take the place of the genuine fact, whose content hash differs.
  • Chain head not anchored outside the database (see the policy history).
  • Approvals are records, not electronic signatures. Re-authentication and signature manifestation are not built.
  • Host operator. In the prototype the administrator also operates the host, which is break-glass access to the superuser and the Keycloak console. Statements by the database superuser are logged in full.
  • One qa person may create and sign off the same access review. This is a known single-person control.
  • Recorded self-check. The test account sergio_qa belonged to the same person as the account svieira. It was granted qa, confirmed account decision #3 (unit UNIT02) and was then deactivated. That confirmation is recorded as independent although it was not. It is noted here and was not undone.

Who reaches production data, and how

Production data here means telemetry, runs and their logs, and the configuration the units run. Each path below is the only way the listed roles reach that data; a role not listed for a path has no way in through it. The roles are those of the access policy on this install (python3 apps/iam/compiler/cli.py hosts).

PathRolesWhat, and at which levelWhat is recorded
Run Monitoroperator (their units only), production_manager, maintenance, qc, qp, engineer, auditor, qa (which includes auditor's rights); bio_scientist and control_scientist pass its gate but may not read runs, so it shows them nothing usefulRuns and live telemetry, ReadEvery request carries the person's verified sign-in and is checked against the route table; reads are not logged one by one.
Configuration UI and the database APIEvery platform role, each with its own database grants and row rules (operators: their units only)Master data and configuration; writes and approvals for the roles that hold themEach change is stamped with the person and kept in the change history; approvals name the approver.
Superset (since 8 November 2026)bio_scientist, control_scientist, engineer (builders, with SQL Lab); production_manager, qc, qp (viewers)Master data and telemetry of every unit, Read, through Superset's own database account svc_superset (no runs); SQL Lab runs any query that account may runSuperset's own log in its database superset; the database sees svc_superset, not the person (as for Grafana). SQL Lab queries are not in the platform's record; published dashboards are not reviewed (N11).
Grafana dashboardsengineer (Editor); auditor, maintenance, production_manager, qa, qc, qp (Viewer)Telemetry of every unit, Read, through Grafana's own database accountGrafana's own log only; the database sees Grafana's account, not the person (a known gap).
Database Management exportauditor, qa, qp, each only for the record groups their role may export (qp: telemetry, runs and the audit histories; auditor and qa: those and the master data, devices, recipes, schedules and account records)A file of whole tables, ExportEvery export in the export log (who, which tables, row counts, the file's checksum), which nobody can change. The file leaves the platform; what happens to it afterwards is not recorded.
AI workbench notebooksbio_scientist, control_scientist, engineer and qa (telemetry and master data, qa also runs, through auditor's rights); admin may open the workbench but reads nothing regulated; not auditor or operatorRead only, through the database API with the person's own sign-in, and only while IAM_POSTGREST_JWT and IAM_DB_ROLES are both trueEach read runs as the person in the database; nothing is logged per read. Outputs are removed from commits to git; what a person's code sends elsewhere is not recorded (a known gap).
MQTT ExplorerengineerLive messages of every unit as they arrive, not stored data; sending only to a unit flagged for commissioning (an engineer proposes it in the Configuration UI's Units tab, qa approves it)Under IAM_MQTT_PERSON, each personal credential in the policy history; before 31 October 2026, one shared account, removed on 1 November 2026.
Node-RED editorengineerThe ingest flows and the live messages; flow code can read Node-RED's database password (a known gap)Each deploy of flows, with the person's name, in Node-RED's audit log; flows outside the repository are reported by the health check.
pgAdminadminNo production data: the schema and the few configuration and policy tables the administrator's database role may readpgAdmin's own log.
The host shell (break-glass)Whoever operates the hostEverything, as the database superuserEvery superuser statement in the database server's log; see the host operator gap.

Decision record

Decisions taken for IAM 2.6, Phase 3 and the approval and commissioning screens, with the reason for each.

DecisionChoiceWhy
