Results, 4 November 2026: E17 version 5 by admin, approved by svieira (qa; a different person_id, not the planned sergio_qa), withdrawn; E18 version 6 proposed --by admin from commit fa81d0c, approved by sergio_qa with the attestation, withdrawn by system:apply. Both prove the mechanism, not independent review (see E17, E18).Decided by the platform owner on 4 November 2026 (owner decisions 2 and 4); see the test accounts.
The approval is verified at apply (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)apply.sh N verifies the stored approval token on the host: an RS256 signature against the realm key Keycloak publishes at that moment (the key is recorded in the applied event as jwk), the issuer, audience, client, type, subject and person of the record, and a token id (jti) used by no other approval. Residual: a token is a sign-in, not a signature over the version (what binds it is the diff digest the database stored with it), and a confirm or dispute token could be reused within its five-minute life; only approvals are checked for reuse. Evidence: exercise E19, 5 November 2026 (training chapter, "Last done"): version 13, approved by sergio_qa (event 199), verified on the host and applied (event 203); apply.sh --audit 13 re-verified the token against the recorded key.Design of slice 4.5 (OA-b, §14.8.5): the database cannot verify a signature, the host can.
The approver must still be eligible at apply (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)Read in Keycloak at apply and again right after the confirmation question, just before the transaction: the approver's account enabled, holding an approver role of the applied policy's dual_control, the approved person_id, the person of none of the authors, and of no enabled admin account (I17; a disabled one does not refuse); and the version widens no role held by any enabled account of that person, its included roles counted. Residual: the seconds between that re-read and the commit. Evidence: exercise E19, 5 November 2026 (training chapter, "Last done"): sergio_qa read eligible at the dry run and again before the transaction of version 13.Owner decisions of 4 November 2026 (OA-b): applied means an approver who is eligible when it takes effect, not only when they approved.
The version applied is the version approved (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)The database transaction compiles the grants and the policy's functions from version N's own file (cli.py --staged), which apply.sh builds from the database rows, checks against them (entries digest in SQL and in Python, the body from the rows) and pins by SHA-256 for the length of its lock; the transaction asserts the entries digest again before and after it marks the version applied. A version whose key snapshot is older than the accepted skeleton applies when its recomputed diff is byte for byte the approved one (owner decision 2(b)).Owner decisions 1 and 2 of 4 November 2026.
Rolling back, and its bound (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)apply.sh --rollback-to K restores a superseded version that a qa person confirmed (and did not dispute) as a new version of kind rollback, applied at once and confirmed afterwards by a qa person other than the one who ran it. It is refused when K's rows under today's skeleton give any role more than under the skeleton K was approved under (OA-c); rows naming a retired group or role are dropped and counted. Pending account decisions are listed, not refused. Evidence: exercise E19, 5 November 2026 (training chapter, "Last done"): version 14 restored version 12 (event 215) and was confirmed by svieira, who did not run it (event 216); the health check warned until then.OA-c: a rollback restores what was approved, never more; confirmed after the fact because the point of a rollback is speed.
A failed rollout is reverted, a skeleton version is not (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)After three failed attempts a change or rollback version is reverted in a second transaction, which files the unfinished revert under the previous version first, so an interruption at any point is resumable (--resume converges forward, never reverts). What a revert does not undo: retired MQTT person credentials, pgAdmin sessions ended by a claims change, narrowings access-api applied in the window (health WARNs until qa reviews them). A skeleton version's failed rollout is left partial_apply {mixed}: the accepted skeleton moved and HEAD carries it; undoing it is a git revert plus a deploy, which accepts it as a narrowing.Owner decision 3 of 4 November 2026.
The health baseline of an apply (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)Before the question, apply.sh runs the artefact checks it runs after the apply (eight; nine from Superset stage C, which adds Superset roles). For apply.sh N any FAIL refuses ("fix them first"); for a rollback it is reported and never drives a revert. After the apply only a check that was not FAIL before counts.Owner decision 13: a check failing for reasons no policy version causes must not revert a correct apply.
Dual control read from the policy (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)The User Manager takes who approves and who makes account and policy changes from the route table's dual_control, compiled from the policy, instead of its own list; without the key it keeps qa and admin.One source of the rule (S-E1).
The history's head outside the database (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)The policy history's head (event id and hash) is written into the apply log, into every applied event (chain_head_before) and into each nightly backup's MANIFEST. Residual: a superuser who disables the triggers and re-hashes the chain from an edited event onward is found only by comparing with those copies (§16 of the design), not by verify_chain().S-F1: anchor the head where the database's superuser cannot rewrite it.
Role composites at apply (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)apply.sh compares Keycloak's composite roles with the accepted skeleton's includes ("Keycloak's role R includes …, the accepted skeleton …: ./deploy-infra.sh adds the composites") and refuses a skeleton version that changes includes ("not applied in 4.5"): ./deploy-infra.sh only adds composites, so nothing could apply the change.Owner decision 4 of 4 November 2026: compiling the composites from the policy is left to a later slice.
A rotated realm key, and someone left to approve (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)An approval whose signing key Keycloak no longer publishes is refused with "withdraw version N and draft again" (an approved version cannot be returned). After the version, an enabled account must still hold an approver role of iam_policy and of iam_users whose person is not an enabled maker's: a refusal for apply.sh N, a warning for --rollback-to, which must not be blocked and is confirmed afterwards.Owner decisions 6 and 7 of 4 November 2026.
Reuse of an approval token (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)A token id (jti) is refused only when another version's approved evidence holds it. Accepted residual: a captured confirm or dispute token could be replayed at an approve within its 300-second life.Owner decision 12 of 4 November 2026: the strict rule would refuse an honest approve made after a confirm in the same session.
How the approval check is tested (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)The signature and Keycloak checks are tested offline (fixed RS256 vectors, a fake Keycloak) and live (tests/iam-policy.sh --apply, exercise E19); the throwaway database fixture runs the bundle with unsigned evidence. Production code has no second, test-only key path. The live runs found what the offline tests could not: PostgREST stores the claims with the role it took (anon), so the exact comparison refused every real approval at apply (found by tests/iam-policy.sh --change, fixed in d1a4c48) and failed the audit of a real approval (found by E19, fixed the same day); both now decide by one rule, source.claims_recorded, which accepts that one added key and nothing else.Owner decision 8 of 4 November 2026.
A deploy after an unfinished rollout (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)./apps/iam/deploy.sh resumes an apply left at apply_started by itself, but only warns on partial_apply ("ended in partial_apply: ./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume --by <you>"): a mixed or reverting outcome wants a person to look first.Owner decision 9 of 4 November 2026.
The backup's chain head, read before the dump (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)The nightly job reads the policy history's head before pg_dump, so the dump holds at least that event; a restore whose chain ends below it, or carries another hash there, was cut or rewritten after the backup (backups.sh restore-help prints the comparison). An exact snapshot (pg_dump --snapshot) would need a held connection in the job's shell.Owner decision 10 of 4 November 2026.
What exercise E19 changes on this install (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)E19 narrows one cell of a role no account on this install holds (maintenance or qc), chosen with the live test's guard (only routes and grants change), and rolls it back. Its effect is shown by the applied event's changed list, the moved route-table digest and the role's lost privilege, not by a person's refusal. As in E16 to E18, its accounts belong to one human, so it proves the mechanism, not independent review. Done 5 November 2026 with maintenance R on device_history (versions 13 and 14).Owner decision 11 of 4 November 2026: the full mechanism, no effect on anyone's access.
The Node-RED editor's Logout signs out of the platform (5 November 2026)The editor's Logout continues, after the editor has ended its own session, through the same chain as the user menu's Sign out: Node-RED's sign-in gate, the platform sign-in's "Do you want to log out?" page (client node-red), then the AI Workbench's logout when the workbench is installed, landing on the platform sign-in page. The address is fixed at deploy (NR_LOGOUT_URL), holds no sign-in token, and the editor takes only an https address. Decided by the platform owner on 5 November 2026, when the gap was found.Found live during exercise E15: after Logout, opening Node-RED again showed the engineer's flows at once. Logout ended only the editor's session; the sign-in gate's cookie and the platform sign-in stayed, and the editor's automatic sign-in took the same person straight back in. The next person on that browser could have acted, and deployed, under the engineer's name. The workbench had the same gap until 1 November 2026. Exercise E21 checks it.
Boards reach the broker over TLS only (5 November 2026)Boards connect to the broker on port 31884, TLS only. Each board checks the broker's certificate against the platform's certificate authority, copied to it at onboarding, and by the name mqtt.<domain>, before it sends its password. The certificate is issued by ./deploy-infra.sh from the same authority as the web certificate. The plain port 31883 was closed at once, not after a transition. Each message is not signed in addition: a publish is trusted because the board signed in over TLS with its own password and stays within its own slot's topics. Decided by the platform owner on 5 November 2026.Each board already had its own password and topic limits, but the password crossed the network in clear at every connection, so anyone on the network could capture it and publish as the board. No board was registered on the platform at the time, so closing the plain port at once cut nobody off. Signing every message would also guard against something inside the platform publishing forged readings, at the cost of key handling on the board, in Node-RED and in onboarding; the owner judged sign-in over TLS enough. Tried on an ESP32-S3 before it was built: the right certificate connects; a wrong name, a wrong authority, an expired certificate and a board clock at 2000 are refused. The health check's Mosquitto MQTT (TLS) watches it. Exercise E22 checks it; on 6 November 2026 in part: plain port closed, certificate verified by name, a board registered with the TLS settings; its own connection waits for its sensor (the board restarts before connecting while no sensor answers).
Onboarding checks the WiFi passphrase at once (5 November 2026)Right after the passphrase, the freshly flashed board joins the network itself; the run goes on only when it got an address, or when the person chooses to continue anyway. The passphrase field has a Show button. Files are copied with boot.py last and each copy is retried. Asked for by the platform owner on 5 November 2026.An onboarding ended with "wrong passphrase" after every file had been written. The passphrase was right: every copy restarts the board, which ran the boot.py already copied and started a WiFi sign-in that the next copy cut off, and after a dozen cut-off sign-ins the access point refused the board for minutes. The copy tool's errors were also discarded, and the last check ended on an error before the run's summary. All are fixed (training chapter, E22).
Back and Cancel in onboarding (5 November 2026)Back only on the questions before the board is touched (role, slot, wiring) and on the WiFi network and passphrase; Cancel at every step until the board's files are written, for the person who started the run only, never inside a flash write; after that the run always goes on to register the board and write its record, so the passwords just put on the board are kept. The platform's database is written only at the end of a run, so Back and Cancel leave no record behind; a cancelled run says what state the board was left in. Asked for by the platform owner on 5 November 2026, who chose Back before the erase only.A wrong answer in the planning questions meant abandoning the run in the browser, which left the script waiting. Back after the erase would re-ask questions whose effect on the board cannot be undone, so it is not offered there. Exercise E23 checks it; done on 6 November 2026 as expected. It also found that the wizard page's sign out left the portal's own session open for up to 4 minutes; since that day it follows the platform's one-hop sign-out (Keycloak, the AI Workbench, the portal), as the user menu does; checked live the same day.
Configuration records are retired, never deleted (5 November 2026)The Configuration UI has no Delete for locations, units, zones, devices or components; each form says to set Status to Inactive. Onboarding a slot again retires the earlier board's components instead of deleting them. Asked for by the platform owner on 5 November 2026.The access policy gives no person a DELETE grant on platform data (level D: records are retired), so under IAM_DB_ROLES=true every such Delete was refused, and a re-onboarding failed at its registration ("permission denied for table component", found that day). A retired record keeps the history, including the board's slot history.
Health and test messages are stored (6 November 2026)A SENSE board's health message (…/sense/_health) is stored in medcea.measurement with type HB, and a new test message (tag _test) with type TS. Both carry a reading's fields plus the board's IP and MAC address. Every board sends one test message at start-up; the host sends one as the board on request (the wizard's Send test message, flash-device.sh --send-test). The ingest flow takes the type from the topic, never from the message: only exactly sense/_health is HB and only sense/_test or control_setpoint/_test is TS; a message elsewhere that names either type is dropped with a warning in Node-RED's log. Migration 009 replaces the type's database check with the exact list AP, CT, SP, HB, TS. A sensor that fails no longer restarts the board: the health message says which one and why. Decided by the platform owner on 6 November 2026 (stored, the two types, the three senders); the topic rule's exact form and the drop by the implementer in the review the same day.The health message was built with the wiring screen, but the database's check refused it, so a sensor that failed showed nowhere but on the board's console; before that, a board with no working sensor restarted every 15 seconds and never connected (exercise E22). A test message proves a board's whole path (credential, topic rights, TLS, ingest) without waiting for a reading, and must be findable in the broker and in the database. Taking the type from the topic means no message, whatever it says about itself, can be counted as a reading or as a test that it is not. The old check was three pattern matches (a value containing AP, CT or SP, held to those three only by the column's two characters), not a list; rows outside the new list would leave the new check unvalidated (new rows still checked) with a warning rather than fail the deploy. The readers (Run Monitor, Grafana dashboards, the measurement views) select readings, commands and reports by type, so they show neither new type. Exercises E25 and E26 check it.
Hubs on one bus: the board closes the other hub's channel (review, 6 November 2026)The wiring check allows the same sensor address behind two different hubs on one bus (and behind two channels of one hub). The board makes that safe: before a hub opens a channel, every other hub on the bus closes its own; if one does not answer, the read is refused, naming that hub's address, rather than two sensors answering at once.Found in the review of the wiring screen: the check already allowed it, which is why a second hub is used, but the board left the other hub's channel open, so two sensors at one address could answer together. Fixing it on the board keeps the wiring the screen allows; refusing it in the check would have refused the reason for a second hub.
The SEN0562 light sensor's mode is written before every read (6 November 2026)The board writes the sensor's continuous high-resolution mode (0x10, the command of DFRobot's own example) before every reading, waits 180 ms and reads two bytes; lux is the raw value divided by 1.2.Found in the review: the sensor (a BH1750 inside) comes back from a power loss switched off and still answers with its last value, so a mode written once would publish a frozen reading with nothing to say it is wrong. The plan had named the one-time mode (0x20); the implementer kept DFRobot's command, written each time, which also starts a fresh measurement at every read. Whether it runs at 3.3 V is a bench check (exercise E25).
The bench-tested hub wiring is the shipped starting point (7 November 2026)The owner's I2C hub bench test (i2c_hub_test.py rev3, 6 November 2026, on the ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1) passed with: hardware I2C(0) on GPIO 8 / 9 at 100 kHz with a 250 ms timeout, a TCA9548A at 0x70 (SparkFun Qwiic Mux BOB-16784) alone on the root bus, the SHT45 on channel 7, the SCD30 on channel 6, channels 0 to 5 empty. The platform ships that wiring as the board template Sense board as bench-tested 6 Nov 2026. The board firmware takes the test's timings on hardware I2C: a 250 ms bus timeout, an SHT45 soft reset at start and a read retried while the sensor is still converting, 4 ms between an SCD30 command and its read (the library's 1 ms is too short), and the SCD30's measurement interval set to 2 s before it starts, written only when the sensor holds another value (it is kept in the sensor's flash). For the owner to confirm (the implementer's choices, not part of the request): the wiring check no longer warns against the SCD30 on hardware I2C; software I2C gets the same 250 ms timeout, which is set but was never bench-tested (the test ran hardware I2C only); and the design map (SHT45 ch0, SCD30 ch1, SEN0562 ch2) stays as a second template, now on hardware I2C.The platform owner asked on 7 November 2026 for "a template that works", on the evidence of the bench test; the shipped bench template is that decision. The rest of this row is the implementer's reading of the test, listed for the owner to confirm. Software I2C with the SCD30, the SEN0562 and the chamber design map are not bench-tested yet; E25 records the first onboarding with the bench template.
Engineers' test messages from the MQTT Explorer (6 November 2026)Planned, not built. An engineer may send a test message to a board's sense/_test topic from the MQTT Explorer only after an approved skeleton version of the access policy adds it (proposed with apply.sh --propose-skeleton, approved by qa in the Access Policy, applied with apply.sh N), under the same condition as commands: only for a unit flagged for commissioning. Until then tests are sent from the wizard and the host only.The platform owner asked for this third sender on 6 November 2026. A person may today write only a commissioning unit's control topics; a sense topic gives a role more access, which the skeleton gate refuses on every deploy, so it can come only as an approved version (IAM 4.5).
AppArmor rules for containers on newer Ubuntu kernels (8 November 2026)The installer adds rules to MicroK8s's container profile instead of loosening the host: ./deploy-infra.sh installs a root-owned script and two systemd units that rebuild /etc/apparmor.d/cri-containerd.apparmor.d from MicroK8s's own profile plus four rules (signal and ptrace between processes of a container, with the plain and the stacked label, as the fix proposed upstream in containerd issue 14485), whenever MicroK8s rewrites it, and turn off Ubuntu's host profile mosquitto while the host has no Mosquitto of its own. kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_unconfined stays 1 and no pod runs unconfined. A health check (Container AppArmor, the first) fails while the rules are missing or a signal is refused inside a container. The host stays on kernel 7.0.0-38 until exercise E29 passes on the newer kernel. Decided by the platform owner on 8 November 2026. Installed on 9 November 2026 (E29 steps 1–4 on 7.0.0-38: units active, the rules put back within 4 seconds after a containerd restart, a second deploy changes nothing, all 57 health checks OK). E29 passed on the newer kernel the same day (steps 5–7): on 7.0.0-43 PostgreSQL ran under the stacked label the rules cover, 0 signals refused, Container AppArmor OK with no health failure; 7.0.0-43 is now the default kernel and the hold on 7.0.0-38 is lifted.Kernels 7.0.0-42 and 7.0.0-43 took the whole platform down on 8 November 2026: PostgreSQL hung in crash recovery, nginx could not reload, Mosquitto could not read its configuration. Setting the sysctl to 0 would turn off a hardening default for every program on the host, and running pods unconfined would drop their AppArmor confinement entirely; both were rejected. Writing the profile once would not last, because MicroK8s's containerd wrapper copies its own profile over it at every start, and containerd keeps a profile of that name once one is loaded, so the units put the rules back after each copy. The host profile mosquitto confines nothing on this host, which runs no Mosquitto of its own; if one is installed, it stays on and the health check names the container it attaches to. Known gap: until containerd ships its fix, each MicroK8s refresh relies on the profile still ending with its closing brace; the script refuses to change a profile of another shape, and the check fails.
Dialog boxes for ./guide.sh, the name ./medcea.sh, the end-of-command box and the MedCEA logo (9 November 2026)At a terminal the menus' questions are whiptail dialog boxes, each menu headed by a read-only status header (host, kernel, git commit, the last health check, the applied policy version, the deploy lock, the dry-run banner); the commands still run on the plain terminal. --plain, MEDCEA_PLAIN=1 (GUIDE_PLAIN=1 still accepted) and piped input keep the numbered mode unchanged. Then, the same day: the rename: ./guide.sh became ./medcea.sh, named after the platform, MedCEA, and not after PROJECT_NAME (an install with another project name runs ./medcea.sh too); ./guide.sh is kept for now as a forwarding alias that says so on stderr and runs ./medcea.sh with the same options and exit code, to be removed in a later release; every instruction, message and hint names ./medcea.sh, and the config.env.guide-<timestamp>.bak backups keep their name. The end-of-command box: with util-linux script installed, a command runs under script (its own terminal, so colours, sudo and its own questions work as before) and, when it ends, a box titled "Finished: exit code 0" or "Failed: exit code N" shows the command, the log it wrote and the last lines of its output, with Menu and Quit; a switch recipe or Bring IAM to full enforcement shows one box at its end, for all its steps; without script, the Enter prompt as before. The MedCEA logo: deploy-infra's banner moved into infra/lib-banner.sh; a compact version heads the first menu on a large terminal (never a sub-menu, left out when there is no room), the numbered mode prints the full one once at a terminal.Owner's choice: easier to read and harder to mis-type than numbered lists, with the platform's state in view before each choice. The questions, the checks on answers, the confirmations (a change defaults to No, a destructive command still wants yes typed) and what runs and is logged are the same in both modes; the header only reads files on the host, so it can neither change nor hold anything. Cancel or Esc in a question leaves the action with nothing run, and a box that fails ends the menus (exit 1): neither is ever taken as an answer (review of 9 November 2026). The name (owner's decision): the tool belongs to the platform, so its name must not change with an installation's project name; the alias spares existing notes and habits for one transition. The end box (owner's decision): the result and the output's end stay readable after the box clears the screen. What script records can include anything the command printed on the terminal, so the file is private (mode 600 in a mode-700 folder), read into memory and deleted as soon as the box is built, never kept, copied or logged; output holding the credentials box gets no box at all (the credentials stay on the terminal, and their text never reaches the box's command line, which other local accounts could read). The commands keep the deploy lock and its environment exactly as before (a recipe's steps still run under its one lock). Under script, Ctrl+C reaches only the command; a recipe step stopped so still stops the recipe (exit 130). The logo's tagline is now cyan, as always intended (the old check looked for "Medical"). Exercise E30.
Health checks of Phase 5: proving the applied policy is the one in force (9 November 2026)Scope of this round: four new checks, iamloaded (every running pod of the six route-checking services loaded the ConfigMap's route table), jwks (the Secret medcea-jwks holds exactly the realm's signing keys; always on; the key-id comparison moved here from postgrest, so a stale key fails once, not twice), kcscopes (the groups and medcea-identity scopes, their mappers, and both as default scopes on every platform client, read from Keycloak's database read-only; one client list, infra/lib-keycloak-clients.sh, for ./deploy-infra.sh and the check) and iamnetpol (the labelled NetworkPolicies by name against the compile), so 61 checks; and changes to existing ones: iamgrants no longer reads a drift as SKIP and, under IAM_DB_ROLES=false, warns of an unclassified table; iammqtt asks every iam-api pod; iampolicy warns when the Policy UI runs another compiler; noderedflows warns of flow files not committed to git; iamenforce fails without an enforce key and compares the switches recorded in settings.json with config.env (the file itself is not changed, so no service re-renders); iamchain warns when verify_chain() is not SECURITY DEFINER or not executable by iam_svc. FAIL only for what lets someone in, breaks token verification or proves a pod runs an outdated route table: a missing groups scope, groups mapper, audience mapper or person_id mapper on a client whose tokens reach a platform API (the User Manager's host clients, the token clients such as workbench-notebook, the onboarding wizard; mqtt-explorer counts, being a host client whose tokens reach iam-api); a realm RS256 key id the Secret lacks, or a Secret key id the realm no longer publishes; jwks-sig.json other than the signing keys of jwks.json; a service pod whose loaded route digest differs from the ConfigMap's for 120 seconds or more, or has none where the service enforces. Everything else WARNs: the same scope problems on a tool-only client (Grafana, pgAdmin, Superset, Node-RED, the workbench), an optional-only scope, full_scope_allowed off, uncommitted flow files, switches in settings.json other than config.env, an unclassified table under IAM_DB_ROLES=false, verify_chain() not SECURITY DEFINER or not executable by iam_svc, another compiler, IAM_NETPOL false (with or without labelled policies left), and a check that cannot read its source (a missing Secret medcea-jwks still FAILs). A realm that does not answer is a WARN in jwks, worded as the realm's problem (the Keycloak checks already FAIL it). The 120 seconds are counted from the ConfigMap's newest managedFields time (a time that cannot be read counts as past the 120 seconds). A pod with the current route digest and an older applied version is OK: the version is information only. Not this round: account drift between Keycloak and the database, an anchor for the chain head, a catalogue of the checks, a test of the documentation (account drift and the anchor came in the second round the same day, with a check of the database catalog: next row). Decided by the platform owner on 9 November 2026. Run on the live platform on 9 November 2026 (exercise E31, commit ed2b13f): all 61 checks OK, the four new ones with the expected texts; an uncommitted flow file WARNed in Node-RED flows vs git and cleared after git checkout.The health check said a policy version was applied, but nothing proved that the pods run its route table, that the keys and claims every token needs are in place, or that IAM_NETPOL is in force; and iamgrants could read real drift as SKIP. Failing on everything that is not final would turn every fresh install red; a FAIL is kept for what admits someone or refuses everyone, so it is acted on at once. Reading Keycloak's database instead of its admin API needs no token, writes no sign-in event and opens no port. Reading each pod with one kubectl exec that prints only a digest needs no change to the services. The four new checks prove the controls are in place, not that they work: tests/iam-hosts.sh, tests/iam-signin.sh and tests/iam-network.sh still test that.
Health checks of Phase 5, round 2: account drift, chain anchor, catalog (9 November 2026)Three new checks, so 64. Severity: the rule of the first round, extended: FAIL also for what proves tampering with, or drift of, the access records; everything else WARNs, and a check that cannot read its source WARNs. iamdrift (Account drift): the User Manager's service (access-api) computes the drift between Keycloak and the account record in the background, every 10 minutes (DRIFT_INTERVAL_SECONDS, never below 60; after a failed run it tries again after 2 minutes), with its existing service account and the one comparison the Decisions tab's banner already used (not a copy of it), in a read-only database session it rolls back and with no Keycloak write. It publishes only counts (accounts, unexplained roles, enabled while pending, failed compensations, unrecorded accounts), when it computed, whether the account list was cut, whether the seeded accounts could be read, and the kind of the last error: never a name, username, sub or e-mail. Keycloak's lists are read in pages up to a ceiling of 10000 accounts (before, 2000 at most, silently); reaching it is reported. New kind unrecorded account: an enabled account that no access request, account decision or status change names; service accounts never count. Exempt are seeded accounts only: those with an account_seeded fact (created, person_id_set or observed) on the policy history, matched by sub, by username only for a fact without a sub (./deploy-infra.sh records none without one). Nothing else is exempt: the test accounts of the 1 November install show until they are reviewed, as expected; the platform admin ADMIN_USER counts as seeded: the owner named it among the seeded accounts, and since 10 November 2026 ./deploy-infra.sh records it like the first qa person and the first engineer (a created fact when it creates it, else the one-time observed fact), so this round needs ./deploy-infra.sh once before ./apps/access/deploy.sh. (Built at first with an extra exemption, an account the latest signed-off access review listed; removed in review the same day, since the owner exempted seeded accounts only and the exemption lapsed at the next sign-off anyway.) A seeded account's role is explained by its seed fact: the role of its created fact, or for an account with none, its first observed fact (the one-time record of QA_USER, ENGINEER_USER and ADMIN_USER as they were); a later observed fact, which ./deploy-infra.sh records when it sees the role changed, explains nothing, so a role added in Keycloak outside the record is not laundered by the next deploy. Without this, a fresh install's seeded qa and engineer accounts would FAIL Account drift. A later decision replaces the seeded role as any later record does. The check reads the counts with one bounded, read-only kubectl exec into the access pod: FAIL on an unexplained role or a failed compensation; WARN on an account enabled while pending, an unrecorded account, a result older than 30 minutes, an error, a cut list, a fresh pod, and an access-api that predates the report, until ./apps/access/deploy.sh. iamanchor (History chain anchor): the chain head the newest complete nightly backup recorded in its MANIFEST (read before the dump since IAM 4.5) must still be in iam_policy.history with the same hash, read in one read-only session; FAIL when the event is missing or its hash differs; WARN when there is no backup or MANIFEST, the head cannot be read, the newest backup is older than 48 hours, or the backup folder is unreadable (it is mode 700: the check runs as the account that deployed the backup, never with sudo). After a restore from an older backup it FAILs until the next nightly backup. When the newest backup completed before the history's first event was written (a backup of an earlier database: BACKUP_DIR is kept across a new install and --purge-data), it WARNs that there is no anchor until the next nightly backup instead of comparing two unrelated chains (found in review the same day); someone able to rebuild the whole history with a newer first event therefore gets this WARN, not a FAIL. What it does not prove: someone with superuser rights in the database and access to the host could alter both the history and the backup folder, and a change between two backups is seen only at the next one. iamcatalog (Database catalog): FAIL on any object of medcea, medcea_auth, iam_policy or iam not owned by medcea_owner, any protective trigger (the iam freeze and append-only triggers, the append-only, no-truncate and retired-guard triggers, user_unit_audit_trg, commissioning_history_trg) not ENABLE ALWAYS, and any medcea view without security_invoker, with the exact statements of tests/iam-db.sh (a test compares the two texts); one read-only query, counts and the first five object names. Adapted from the test fixture: the fixture's trigger counts are not checked (they pin the fixture's build), so a dropped trigger is not seen, only a disabled one; iamgrants does not see it either (it compares only the iam_ guard triggers of medcea). Also: tests/iam-hosts.sh asks kubectl for managedFields explicitly, the fix the first round made in the health check. apply.sh's nine checks are unchanged. Decided by the platform owner on 9 November 2026. Run on the live platform on 10 November 2026 (exercise E32, commit 0133421): 64 checks, 63 OK; History chain anchor and Database catalog OK on their first live run; Account drift WARNed one unrecorded account (no unexplained role: the admin role is explained by the seed fact ./deploy-infra.sh recorded that morning): the demo account viewer, which admin deactivated the same morning (decision 19; see the test accounts), after which Account drift was OK with 0 unrecorded accounts.The first round proved the applied policy is in force; it did not prove that the people in Keycloak are the ones the record says, that the history was not shortened, or that the database's protections were not switched off. The drift was visible only to someone who opened the Decisions tab; computing it in the background keeps the health check read-only (it mints no token and reads no names) and the counts carry nothing personal into the logs. Exempting only seeded accounts keeps the rule simple and makes every other account explain itself once. The anchor is the only copy of the head outside the database, so it catches a cut or rewritten history that verify_chain() alone cannot see (a shortened chain still verifies). The catalog's statements were proven on the fixture; using the same text keeps one definition of what "protected" means.
Nightly backups to a local folder (1 November 2026)One CronJob (apps/backup), daily at 02:30 UTC: pg_dump in custom format of the platform database and Keycloak's, the roles without passwords, and a copy of every AI workbench home, Node-RED's /data and Grafana's volume, into one dated folder per run in BACKUP_DIR on the host (default /var/backups/medcea, mode 700), with sizes, SHA-256 checksums and an OK marker written last. Folders older than BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS (14) are deleted after a good run, never the newest complete one. No uninstall deletes the folder. The health check warns after 26 hours without a complete backup and fails after 72. The restore is a documented, manual procedure (./apps/backup/backups.sh restore-help); no script runs it. Decided by the platform owner on 1 November 2026.Nothing backed up the workbench homes, Grafana's database or Node-RED's data, and the databases only through a manual export; the owner wants a copy from which a person's lost work or the whole platform can come back. A local folder needs no other service or credential; on its own disk it survives a reinstall and the mistakes it guards against, and the owner can point it at another disk. The restore stays manual because it stops services and drops databases, and what to put back (one home, or everything after a reinstall) is a decision a script cannot take safely. The job reads the volumes' whole directory read-only rather than each volume, so a new person's home is copied from its first night without a redeploy. Same host and disk is listed as a known gap. Exercise E12 in the training chapter checks a backup and a restore.
Unit assignment in the User Manager (12 November 2026)Reverses owner decision 4 of IAM 4.1 (units stay in units.sh): an admin assigns and removes an operator's units in the account's Units section, through the access service's database function iam.record_unit_decision; an assignment still waits for a qa person who is neither maker nor subject, and a removal applies at once. The owner's choices: both routes are admin only (K on unit assignments; at first qa and auditor were to read an account's units too, reversed the same day, see below); an assignment to an account that is not an operator, is disabled or has no person_id is refused with the reason, while removing a leftover unit stays allowed for any account; units.sh stays as the host and break-glass path (--bootstrap, an account Keycloak no longer has). The two routes widen the skeleton, so the change ships as an approved skeleton version. After the review the owner made the read route admin only (12 November 2026): the first proposal gave qa and auditor the read route, so it widened qa's own reach, and the approval rule refuses an approver whose role, or a role it includes, gains reach; only qa approves policy versions, so it could never have been approved. qa still sees every unit decision in the Decisions tab. Who may see an account's permissions stays open. The general consequence: under the current approval rule, no change that widens qa's own reach (or auditor's, which qa includes) can be approved by qa. The owner also kept two points as built: a production_manager counts as an operator and may be assigned units, although they already work in every unit; an administrator may assign a unit to a second account of their own person, since the qa person who confirms must be neither maker nor subject. Evidence: applied as skeleton version 3 on 12 November 2026 (proposed from commit 18bec35, approved by qa_user); exercise E2 the same day: decision 3 assigned UNIT01 to oper and qa_user confirmed it (history events 38 and 39), an assignment to the engineer account was refused (409, nothing recorded), and decision 4 removed it at once (event 40).Assigning units on the host made the administrator's claim of who they are (--by) unprovable, so every such row needed a qa attestation and the work needed host access. In the User Manager the maker is the signed-in administrator, the reason is required, and dual control is the same as for every other account decision. Refusing a non-operator, a disabled account or one without a person keeps assignments that could never take effect, or could not be tied to a person, out of the record; qa and auditor check what they confirm and review in the Decisions tab.
The Configuration UI follows the database's own answer (12 November 2026)No policy change, no new route, no skeleton version: only the page changes. Panels read with error-driven reads: a panel whose main read the database refuses (42501) says in plain words that the role does not read it; a secondary read (control algorithms in the Recipe ↔ Unit grid, device counts in the Zones panel) may fail and the panel shows less, with a note. Write controls follow one zero-row write probe per table the page writes (a PATCH naming a record that does not exist, sent once when the page opens): where the database refuses it, New, Edit, Import, the grid's grant and settings buttons, Copy, Retire, Save to Platform Library and Onboard Device are hidden, not greyed out; a read-only record opens with View. Any other answer keeps today's behaviour (the control shows and the database decides). Constraint refusals (drafts only, approved recipes only, existing slots) and the platform library's route-gate refusals keep coming at save time, now in plain words. A device import carries no zone, so maintenance's device import is always refused by the existing-slot rule, with a sentence saying so: the probe cannot tell a constrained right from a full one, so the button stays. A probe that does not answer within 4 seconds counts as unknown, and the controls stay invisible until the probes have answered. Exercise E33. Open items found, not fixed here: the scheduler's GET /api/units shows the number of allowed recipes and learned-state records to roles that read neither recipes nor controller state (admin, maintenance, qc, qp), a scheduler or policy change; the grid's Permission Settings still writes the legacy algorithm_id and algorithm_params columns, not a parameter set (params_id, migration 008).The owner asked for a fix now, without a policy change. The database stays the only decider and the page needs no role list, so it cannot drift from the policy; under IAM_DB_ROLES=false the answer is truthful too (every person runs with the same grants, so every person sees the same buttons). Rejected: the PostgREST OpenAPI root (it lists write operations from the table's structure, not the role's privileges, so admin would still see Edit on units); a medcea.my_privileges() function (granted to every role it widens qa's own reach, which qa cannot approve); a compiled capabilities document (a new compile target, digest and health work, the policy's intent rather than the database's answer, and wrong under IAM_DB_ROLES=false); asking PostgREST to roll back each probe (needs a config-api setting that lets any client roll back). Hiding is a convenience for the person, never the control. Cost: about ten extra requests per page load and one "permission denied" line in the PostgreSQL log per refused probe.

Running the platform

This chapter is for the administrator who runs the MedCEA host. It covers installing the platform with ./install.sh, the deploy scripts and the order they run in, the rule that only one deploy runs at a time, and ./medcea.sh, the question-and-answer front end to all of these commands. It then explains the seven IAM switches in config.env that turn the access controls on step by step (and WORKBENCH_ENABLED, which medcea.sh switches the same way), which of them a fresh install leaves off and how to turn those on, what the health check reports, which IAM test scripts to run and what a good result looks like, how operators are given units, how to uninstall, how the domain names reach other devices through Tailscale, and the credentials file. It ends with troubleshooting for problems an administrator can meet. Run every command from the repository root on the host.

Installing and updating

./install.sh is the one entry point. It runs three stages in order: the infrastructure (./deploy-infra.sh), every application (./deploy-apps.sh --all), and the health check (./health-check.sh). While IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is true (a new config.env's default since 8 November 2026) it runs the infrastructure once more between the applications and the health check, and says why ("IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is true: the infrastructure runs once more, so Grafana and pgAdmin move onto their own database roles (svc_grafana, rr_admin_login) now that the database lets them log in."): Grafana and pgAdmin are deployed by the first stage, before the database deploy in the applications stage lets their roles log in. It is the switch's own enable recipe, under the same deploy lock; a failure stops the install like any stage. The same command updates an existing install: finished steps are skipped or updated in place, so it is safe to run again after a pull or after a failure. If a stage fails, the script stops, names the stage and its log file in logs/, and tells you to fix the cause and run it again.

CommandWhat it does
./install.shInstall or update everything: infrastructure, applications, the infrastructure again while IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is true, health check. Asks for any missing settings first.
./install.sh --configureReview every setting (current values offered as defaults), then install.
./install.sh --infra-onlyOnly the infrastructure: MicroK8s, PostgreSQL, Keycloak, Grafana, Node-RED, the portal and the AI workbench.
./install.sh --apps-onlyOnly the applications. Needs the infrastructure and config.env. While IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is true it ends with "Still to do, unless ./deploy-infra.sh has run since this database deploy: ./deploy-infra.sh, so Grafana and pgAdmin move onto their own database roles".
./install.sh --helpThe options, including the uninstall levels (see Uninstalling).

At the end of an install the script prints, in this order: "MedCEA is installed" with the portal's address; while any IAM switch is still false, one line pointing to ./medcea.sh → IAM switches → Bring IAM to full enforcement (see After a fresh install; a fresh install always prints it); when the applications stage skipped Superset, a "Still to do" line saying why and what to run (see Superset); then the steps for trusting the platform's certificate authority on your devices, and the credentials box last, so it stays on screen (see The credentials file).

config.env and the setup questions

All settings live in config.env in the repository root. It is not in git and is readable only by its owner (mode 600), because it holds every platform password. You do not write it by hand: the first run of ./deploy-infra.sh (or ./install.sh) creates it from config.env.example by asking questions. Press Enter to accept the value shown in brackets. Later runs ask only for required values that are still empty. To review every setting, run ./deploy-infra.sh --configure, or ./infra/configure.sh to edit the settings without deploying.

The questions cover:

  • Project name (PROJECT_NAME, default medcea): the MQTT topic root, the Kubernetes namespace and the Keycloak realm. Lowercase, starting with a letter, 2 to 31 characters from a-z 0-9 -. Changing it after boards are flashed means reflashing them.
  • Domain (DOMAIN): every web page is served at <service>.<DOMAIN>. The menu offers a name (for example medcea, so the portal is portal.medcea) when Tailscale is up, the Tailscale or LAN IP with nip.io, or a custom domain you provide DNS for. Changing the domain later means running ./deploy-infra.sh again.
  • The platform administrator: username, a real e-mail address you read (Keycloak password resets go there, and it is the pgAdmin login) and password. Addresses on special-use domains (.local, .test, .invalid, .example, .localhost, .arpa, .onion) are refused here and for the qa person and the engineer: pgAdmin will not start with one.
  • The first qa person and the first engineer: username and e-mail for each. The qa person must be someone other than the administrator. Their initial passwords are generated and replaced at their first sign-in.
  • The PostgreSQL superuser password, the database volume size, and your Docker Hub username and access token (needed to pull the Bitnami Helm charts).
  • On the first run (no config.env yet) and on a full review (--configure): the time zone for Node-RED flows and schedules; the backup folder (BACKUP_DIR, an absolute path, default /var/backups/<project>; better on another disk than the data's, and when you cannot write its parent the applications stage asks for sudo once to create it) and the days to keep backups (BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS); and whether to deploy the AI workbench.

Some values are generated and never asked: the qa and engineer initial passwords, the Keycloak break-glass console account (kc-breakglass) and its password, and the passwords of the database service roles. Configuration also checks for Tailscale on every run. USE_TAILSCALE records whether the domain depends on it: when it is true, a deploy stops if Tailscale is down, rather than quietly falling back to the LAN address.

Password rules

A password you type must be 8 to 64 characters from A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ ~ - only. Other punctuation breaks the URLs and YAML files the password is written into, so the question asks again. Password input is hidden and typed twice. Pressing Enter generates a 20-character password (or keeps the current one if there is one), shows it once, and lists it in the credentials file.

Every command writes its own log in logs/ (readable by the platform user only): deploy-infra-<timestamp>.log, deploy-apps-…, a component deployed on its own app-<component>-deploy-… (or -uninstall-…), app-iam-units-…, deploy-workbench-…, health-check-…, the throwaway database test iam-db-fixture-<command>-… and each live test iam-<name>-…. A command run by another (a component by ./deploy-apps.sh, a test by the fixture) writes into its caller's log. The first line of the output names the file. MEDCEA_NO_LOG=1 turns it off for one run.

Configuration runs before the deploy log starts, so your answers and generated passwords never reach logs/. Its host package check is the exception: when a package is missing, what it reports, its question and apt-get's output go to logs/prereqs-<timestamp>.log (your answer and the sudo password do not), so a deploy stopped there still leaves a record. When configuration rebuilds config.env on a newer config.env.example (keeping your values), it saves the previous file as config.env.bak.

The deploy scripts and their order

install.sh is a thin wrapper. Each stage also works on its own, and after the first install you will usually run the stages directly.

ScriptWhat it deploys
./deploy-infra.shMicroK8s (bootstrapped only on the first run), PostgreSQL, Keycloak with the realm, clients and roles, the MQTT broker, Node-RED, Grafana, pgAdmin, the sign-in proxies, the portal, the AI workbench (unless WORKBENCH_ENABLED=false), the access policy's route table and the realm's public keys. It writes a log to logs/deploy-infra-<timestamp>.log.
./deploy-apps.shA checkbox menu of the application components under apps/. ./deploy-apps.sh --all deploys every component without asking.
./apps/<component>/deploy.shOne component on its own. The components are access, backup (the nightly backup, see Backup and restore), database, edge-wizard, frontend, iam, monitor, mqtt-explorer, node-red, report, scheduler and superset (skipped while the applied access policy gives no role a Superset setting, while IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is not true, and while no version of the policy is applied, see Superset) (./deploy-apps.sh --help lists them).
./infra/deploy-workbench.shRedeploys only the AI workbench (JupyterHub, chart 4.4.4: JupyterHub 5.5.4). A workspace that is already running keeps its old setup until it is stopped and started again. Who may sign in and who is hub administrator come from the access policy; if the policy does not compile, the script stops before it changes anything and the running workbench stays as it is.

The order rules are:

  • Infrastructure first. The applications need the cluster, Keycloak and PostgreSQL that deploy-infra.sh creates. ./install.sh --apps-only refuses without config.env.
  • Database before scheduler. deploy-apps.sh runs components in alphabetical order, so database comes before scheduler. When you deploy them one by one, run ./apps/database/deploy.sh first: the scheduler deploy refuses until the database functions it needs exist.
  • Access after infrastructure. Run ./deploy-infra.sh, then ./apps/access/deploy.sh. The access deploy runs the database deploy itself when it needs to. Since 1 November 2026 the order also matters for Sign out: ./deploy-infra.sh registers the AI Workbench's logout address with each app's sign-in, and the access deploy then points Sign out at it. In the other order, Sign out shows Keycloak's "Invalid redirect uri" and ends nothing until ./deploy-infra.sh has run.
  • After a pull of new IAM code: ./deploy-infra.sh (the route table), then ./apps/database/deploy.sh, then ./deploy-apps.sh --all while no recipe run is active. Until all three have run, the health check's iamgrants and tests/iam-schema.sh stay red.
  • From IAM 4.2a, every deploy that compiles the access policy reads the applied version from PostgreSQL first and refuses while PostgreSQL is not Ready; ./deploy-infra.sh repairs PostgreSQL before it reads the policy, so run it first in that case. A git change that gives access is refused by every deploy (see The skeleton gate).
  • iam-api (the iam component, IAM 3.5) after ./apps/database/deploy.sh and ./apps/access/deploy.sh: alphabetical order already does this. While IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is false (an older config.env) it is skipped with a warning. A new config.env has it true, so a fresh install deploys iam-api and the Access Policy; there, confirming and approving answer "need IAM_POSTGREST_JWT=true and IAM_DB_ROLES=true" until both switches are on. Then turn on IAM_MQTT_PERSON (see IAM switches).
  • After rotating or removing a realm key in Keycloak, run ./deploy-infra.sh. It republishes the keys and restarts config-api when they changed.
  • pgAdmin restarts whenever ./deploy-infra.sh changes its sign-in settings (pgAdmin's client secret, the roles it admits, or ADMIN_PASS), which signs everyone out of pgAdmin; a run that changes none of them leaves it running. Only on an install deployed before 1 November 2026 (not after a fresh install, where the secret never left the Kubernetes Secret): the first ./deploy-infra.sh after that date restarts pgAdmin once, when its secrets move into a Kubernetes Secret, and removes the older copies of pgAdmin's deployment that still held them; pgAdmin's client secret was readable in plain text until then, so give it a new one once: in the Keycloak console, realm medcea, Clients, pgadmin, Credentials, Regenerate; then run ./deploy-infra.sh, which reads the new secret and restarts pgAdmin.
  • pgAdmin's IoT Postgres entry is loaded for each account that may sign in to pgAdmin when pgAdmin starts. ./deploy-infra.sh lists the e-mail addresses of the enabled Keycloak accounts holding a role pgAdmin admits (admin) and gives the list to pgAdmin; when the list changed, pgAdmin restarts (everyone is signed out of it) and loads the entry for each address, which can add several minutes to its start. So after giving someone the admin role, or changing an admin's e-mail address, run ./deploy-infra.sh: until then they can sign in to pgAdmin but see no server. An account without an e-mail address, or with one on a reserved test domain such as .invalid, .test or .example (pgAdmin refuses those), gets no entry; the deploy names it in a warning. If Keycloak cannot be read, the deploy keeps the list pgAdmin already has, so nobody loses their entry, and says so; only when pgAdmin has no list yet does it go on with the platform administrator's address alone. Since 1 November 2026 pgAdmin runs version 9.19.0, pinned in k8s/pgadmin/pgadmin.yaml; on an install from before that date the first ./deploy-infra.sh after it restarts pgAdmin once.
  • Node-RED after ./deploy-infra.sh: when Node-RED's settings changed, the deploy restarts it. Its flows are kept on a volume and survive. The first deploy onto that volume (and a fresh install) starts with no flows; the deploy then says "Node-RED runs no flows" and telemetry is not stored until you run ./apps/node-red/deploy.sh. Do that first deploy while no recipe run is active.

The scheduler runs recipe code straight from the repository (schd/), and the onboarding wizard runs edge/ from it. Do not pull or edit the repository while a recipe run is active: check first that pgrep -af '[r]un_recipe.py' prints nothing.

When your login session is not yet in the microk8s group (for example right after the first install added you to it), the scripts run their microk8s calls through sudo and say why they ask for your password. Log out and back in to stop that.

IAM 4.1: deploying the policy versions schema

Slice 4.1 adds the database side of policy versions (migration 008c), a function the access component installs (iam._changed_since) and every Phase 4 entry of the access policy. Nothing calls them yet. After pulling it, run three deploys in this order, back to back, best through ./medcea.sh → Policy → Deploy IAM 4.1, which holds the deploy lock for all three:

  1. ./apps/access/deploy.sh. It must come first: the database deploy refuses without iam._changed_since ("run ./apps/access/deploy.sh first (IAM 4.1)"), and the health check's iamgrants is red from the pull until this step.
  2. ./apps/database/deploy.sh: migration 008c, the compiled functions and the grants.
  3. ./deploy-infra.sh, at once: the new route table, which the User Manager reads within a minute, and the NetworkPolicies.

From the end of step 2 until the User Manager has read the route table of step 3 (about one to two minutes), the User Manager answers 503 to a grant, an activation, or a role change into qa, qp, admin or auditor: the database and the route table disagree about what such a change widens (the new policy_page row). Do not grant or change roles until all three deploys have finished. A refused decision changed nothing and can simply be repeated. Every other decision and every other service is unaffected.

Between steps 2 and 3 the health check's iamgrants and tests/iam-schema.sh are red; after step 3 and one minute, everything is green. To take slice 4.1 back out, while no policy version exists: run apps/database/medcea_db_migrations_down_008c.sql as postgres in one transaction (the command is in its header), then revert the code, then ./apps/database/deploy.sh and ./deploy-infra.sh; the 503 window opens in reverse. The down file refuses once a version exists.

IAM 4.2a: version 1 and the skeleton gate

Slice 4.2a turns the access policy into numbered versions on this host. The database records version 1 (the factory policy of apps/iam/policy/defaults.yaml, applied at once), every deploy then compiles from the applied version (the host file state/policy-applied.yaml, see Policy source), and every deploy runs the skeleton gate. Nobody's access changes: version 1 compiles to exactly what defaults.yaml compiled to before. After pulling it, check that git status -- apps/iam shows nothing (the bootstrap refuses uncommitted changes there), then run three deploys in this order, back to back, best through ./medcea.sh → Policy → Deploy IAM 4.2a, which asks your username (--by) and holds the deploy lock for all three:

  1. ./apps/database/deploy.sh: the 4.2a database functions (the policy's system actors, the event rules, the filter of the policy history) and the grants. It must come first: the other two record events through these functions.
  2. ./deploy-infra.sh, at once: the route table's digest moves once (it no longer counts the name of the policy file), and the accounts the install seeded are recorded in the policy history (account_seeded, see the policy history).
  3. MEDCEA_POLICY_BOOTSTRAP_BY=<your username> ./apps/iam/deploy.sh: no policy version exists yet, so it runs ./apps/iam/apply.sh --bootstrap --by <you> (without the variable, the platform administrator ADMIN_USER is named). It checks every compile is unchanged, writes version 1 in one database transaction, writes state/policy-applied.yaml, checks the grants, records bootstrap_applied, and restarts iam-api as every iam deploy does.

There is no 503 window: no grant or role changes. Between steps 1 and 2 the health check's iamenforce and tests/iam-schema.sh are red for a few minutes, because the database and the route table disagree about the digest; after step 2 they are green. Step 3 prints [iam] Policy versions..., then the bootstrap's lines (state empty, the tree's commit, the account you named, "version 1 compiles to exactly what defaults.yaml compiles to (N targets): nothing is re-rendered", [policy] state/policy-applied.yaml: version 1 (bootstrap) written, the grants check, the report) and ends "version 1 (bootstrap) applied: nothing was re-rendered". The health check then has two more checks, 54 in all (55 since the Platform manual check of 3 November 2026, 56 since the Superset roles check of 6 November 2026): Access policy version (OK: "version 1 (bootstrap), qa confirms it in the Policy UI once it exists (IAM 4.3)") and Policy artefacts (OK; the Policy UI's host is counted as not deployed). Then run tests/iam-schema.sh and ./apps/iam/apply.sh --status.

If the bootstrap waits (Keycloak not reachable, or a --by that is not an enabled account with a person_id), the iam deploy warns and finishes, and Access policy version FAILs "no applied version: a widening git change is not gated until version 1 exists" until ./apps/iam/deploy.sh runs again. On a fresh install the same happens inside ./install.sh: the iam component bootstraps version 1 in ./deploy-apps.sh --all.

Taking slice 4.2a back out. Version 1 and its events stay in the database, frozen; the down file of 008c refuses while they exist, by design. Under the deploy lock, while the 4.2a code is still there, move the host's policy files aside: bash -c 'source infra/lib-lock.sh && medcea_lock && source infra/lib-policy-source.sh && policy_state_retire rollback' (it moves state/policy-applied.yaml, state/seed-facts.jsonl, state/break-glass/ and the mark state/.policy-versioned into state/retired-<time>-rollback/; the 4.1 code refuses a host file). Then revert the slice in git, run ./apps/database/deploy.sh (the 4.1 functions come back) and ./deploy-infra.sh (the route table's digest moves back once). Applying 4.2a again later finds version 1 and does not bootstrap again.

The applied access policy

From slice 4.2a the access policy in force is the database's applied version, not the file in git. apps/iam/policy/defaults.yaml stays the factory file: version 1 was made from it, and it still holds the platform's skeleton (roles, resource groups and their routes, hosts, the network rules, the invariants: everything but the matrix of who holds which level, and the waivers). The matrix and the waivers come from the applied version.

IAM 4.3: the Policy UI

Slice 4.3 (November 2026) adds the Access Policy at https://policy.<domain>: iam-api serves it on a second port (8083, Service iam-admin) behind its own sign-in proxy (iam-oauth2-proxy, Keycloak client policy). Nobody's access changes and the policy is not changed. Run three deploys in this order, best through ./medcea.sh → Policy → Deploy IAM 4.3 (the Policy UI), which holds the deploy lock for all three:

  1. ./deploy-infra.sh: the Keycloak client policy (with groups, person_id and the medcea-api audience), policy.<domain> in the certificate and the name service, the portal's Access Policy card, and POLICY_DOMAIN, POLICY_CLIENT_SECRET and POLICY_COOKIE_SECRET in config.env.
  2. ./apps/access/deploy.sh: the User Manager's Access Policy link, and Sign out on the new address.
  3. ./apps/iam/deploy.sh: ConfigMap iam-compiler (the policy compiler and the factory file, about 360 KiB, applied server-side), iam-api with its second port, then the sign-in proxy. Like the User Manager's, the proxy admits admin only until every iam-api pod answers on port 8083 that it enforces, then admin, auditor, qa and qp; without that answer the deploy stops with "the Policy UI's gate stays admin-only".

Afterwards the health check has one warning on purpose: Access policy version "version 1 (bootstrap) is not confirmed by qa yet (the Policy UI)", until a qa person confirms it (exercise E16). From then on the check also fails when the Policy UI shows another applied version than the database, and warns when it ships another skeleton than the accepted one (run ./apps/iam/deploy.sh). ./apps/iam/deploy.sh --gate-only re-renders the Policy UI's proxy when it drifted. To remove it: ./apps/iam/uninstall.sh (the proxy, the second port, the compiler ConfigMap and the card); the Keycloak client stays, and a confirmation already recorded stays in the history.

IAM 4.4: drafting and approval

Slice 4.4 (November 2026) lets an admin draft a change to the access policy in the Access Policy and a qa person approve it there, and lets the host operator propose a git skeleton change for the same approval (apply.sh --propose-skeleton, below). Nothing approved is applied in 4.4: applying a version came with slice 4.5 (below). Nobody's access changes, no grant changes and there is no 503 window. Run two deploys in this order, best through ./medcea.sh → Policy → Deploy IAM 4.4 (drafting and approval), which holds the deploy lock for both:

  1. ./apps/database/deploy.sh: the new bodies of the policy's approve and why-not functions (break-glass blocks approvals; a skeleton version needs the attestation, a fresh proposal and an approver whose role it does not widen). No new table, column, function or grant.
  2. ./apps/iam/deploy.sh: iam-api with the write side of the Policy UI, the new page, and ConfigMap iam-compiler with the new diff code (its checksum restarts iam-api).

In the minute between the two the old page still serves and cannot write: harmless. ./deploy-infra.sh and the access deploy are not needed (the route table, the proxies and the clients do not change). Approving needs IAM_POSTGREST_JWT and IAM_DB_ROLES to be true, as confirming does. The health check stays green after the deploy. It WARNs "version N (<kind>) is approved: ./apps/iam/apply.sh N --by <you> applies it" (since slice 4.5; until then "applying it arrives with IAM 4.5") for as long as an approved version waits, "skeleton version N was proposed against skeleton …, the accepted one is now …: return it and propose again" when a deploy accepted a narrowing under a proposal, and, as before, an open version older than 7 days.

Taking slice 4.4 back out.

  1. ./apps/iam/apply.sh --status must show no open change or skeleton version. If one is open, withdraw it: in the Policy UI (an admin, while the 4.4 page still serves), or from the host with ./apps/iam/apply.sh --withdraw-open --by <you> --reason "<why>" (when the page is the reason for the rollback, or after the revert: the 4.3 page has no Withdraw). Last resort, with the 4.4 apply.sh already reverted: SELECT iam_policy._withdraw_open('<reason>') as postgres in the PostgreSQL pod (actor system:apply). An approved 4.4 version must not survive a revert of 4.4: it was approved under 4.4's checks, which the reverted code no longer makes, and slice 4.5 could otherwise apply it.
  2. Revert the slice in git.
  3. The same two deploys.

What stays, by design: the withdrawn and approved versions, their events and their evidence (permanent); a proposed skeleton that was never accepted (harmless). The reverted approve function no longer refuses under break-glass and no longer checks skeleton versions.

IAM 4.5: applying versions

Slice 4.5 (November 2026) applies what a qa person approved: ./apps/iam/apply.sh N --by <you> for a change or skeleton version, ./apps/iam/apply.sh --rollback-to K --by <you> --reason "<why>" to restore an earlier version, and ./apps/iam/apply.sh --audit N to check an applied version afterwards (apply.sh). The deploy itself changes nobody's access, no grant and no gate, and has no 503 window. Run four deploys in this order, best through ./medcea.sh → Policy → Deploy IAM 4.5 (applying versions), which holds the deploy lock for all of them:

  1. ./apps/database/deploy.sh: new_draft refuses a draft while the applied version's last apply event is unfinished (apply_started or partial_apply), whatever events were filed after it.
  2. ./apps/access/deploy.sh: the User Manager reads who approves and who makes account changes from the route table's dual_control, not from a list in its code (proof-gated as before; no access change).
  3. ./apps/iam/deploy.sh: the Access Policy shows the apply states ("applied — rollout incomplete", "approved — a previous apply was reverted") and a rollback's Confirm card; ConfigMap iam-compiler carries the new compiler code, so iam-api restarts.
  4. ./apps/backup/deploy.sh: the nightly backup's MANIFEST names the policy history's head (its id and hash) at the time of the dump.

apply.sh, its checks and health-check.sh run on the host and need no deploy. After the deploy the health check stays green; it WARNs "version N (<kind>) is approved: ./apps/iam/apply.sh N --by <you> applies it" while an approved version waits.

Taking slice 4.5 back out. First ./apps/iam/apply.sh --status: no version may be left apply_started or partial_apply (any outcome: run --resume first), and no open change or skeleton version (withdraw it). Then revert the slice in git and run the same four deploys. The versions applied by 4.5 stay applied and keep their events; the 4.4 code reads them as it reads version 1.

Policy source

Every compile of the policy (every deploy, the health check, the onboarding wizard, flash-device.sh) reads the host file state/policy-applied.yaml when it exists. It is the applied version composed with the accepted skeleton, written by the deploy scripts under the deploy lock: by ./apps/iam/apply.sh after it applies a version, and by every deploy that finds it missing or different from the database. Nobody edits it by hand. state/ is readable by the deploying account only (mode 700, the file 600) and is not in git. Its first two lines say what it is:

# medcea-applied: version=1 kind=bootstrap entries_digest=… skeleton_digest=… git_commit=… written_at=…
# medcea-applied-body: body_digest=… groups=… roles=… dropped=0 keys=…

Every compile checks those lines against the body: a file edited by hand or cut short stops every deploy and the onboarding wizard with "its header does not match its body (edited by hand, or truncated)". Restore it with ./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume --by <you> if an apply was interrupted, or with any deploy, which rewrites it from the database. Health compares the whole body with the database's rows as well (Access policy version).

Before compiling, each deploy reads the applied version from PostgreSQL:

  • No version yet (before the bootstrap, or before migration 008c): the deploy compiles defaults.yaml. A host file at that point is refused: "state/policy-applied.yaml names a version but the database has no policy versions".
  • PostgreSQL not Ready: the deploy refuses and compiles nothing, with or without a host file. ./deploy-infra.sh is the one that repairs PostgreSQL: right after the Kubernetes API answers it only checks the skeleton gate (when the database can be asked; a widening git change stops it there, before anything changes), and it reads the applied policy only after its PostgreSQL step, so run it first. ./deploy-apps.sh asks PostgreSQL once before its first component that compiles the policy and stops the whole run when it is not Ready.
  • A host file without its database (after a restore of an older dump, or a database dropped by hand): restore the database the file belongs to, or move the file aside with policy_state_retire as in Restoring step 2a, only after reading this section. The next deploy then writes it again from the database. apps/database/uninstall.sh --purge-data (after its DROP), ./deploy-infra.sh --reset (after the namespace is gone) and --uninstall (after MicroK8s is removed) do this themselves, under the deploy lock, into state/retired-<time>-<why>/; nothing is deleted.
  • A version was applied here, but the host file is missing: the first host file also writes the mark state/.policy-versioned. While it exists, a compile outside a deploy (the onboarding wizard at its start, flash-device.sh) refuses "state/policy-applied.yaml is absent, but a policy version was applied on this host" instead of falling back to defaults.yaml, which may hold an unreviewed change. The next deploy writes the file again. A restore's step 2a keeps the mark; a deploy that then finds a database with no applied version (a dump older than the bootstrap) moves the mark into state/retired-<time>-no-version/ itself. A purge, a reset and an uninstall move it with the rest.
  • Versions exist but none is applied: refused; see ./apps/iam/apply.sh --status.

What these checks defend against, and what they do not. They stop a widening of access from reaching a deploy through the platform's own tools: a change in git, a variable left exported in a shell, a file edited during a deploy, a stale or hand-edited state/ file, a cold or crashed PostgreSQL, a restore or a purge. They do not stop the account that deploys the platform from going round them on purpose (it can run psql as postgres, edit the scripts, or rewrite the host file with recomputed digests): that is the host operator's break-glass, found afterwards through the policy history, the version audit and the health check, not prevented. A host file forged that way passes the compile's own checks, is found by the health check, and is overwritten by the next deploy; the onboarding wizard can compile it in between (see known gaps).

Two edge cases: flash-device.sh run from another clone of the repository, which has no state/, compiles defaults.yaml (harmless while version 1 equals it; it matters once a later version differs, IAM 4.5). The onboarding wizard compiles once when it starts, so a new applied version reaches it only at its next restart (./apps/edge-wizard/deploy.sh --gate-only restarts it only when its roles changed).

The skeleton gate

Every deploy compares the skeleton in git with the skeleton the platform accepted last. A change that gives access is refused before anything is compiled or changed. It counts as giving access when it adds, for any role: a route, a host, a database privilege or row filter, a tool setting, an MQTT topic or a level; and also, for nobody in particular: a route anyone may call without signing in, an upstream every signed-in host reaches, a host's service or client, a network source allowed into a pod, a host outside the sign-in proxies, a hop or a token client of a calling pod, any privilege or membership of a service identity, any database row filter, and any weakening of the checker's own rules (the invariants, the waivable list, break-glass, the database roles, the levels, the resource types, the classes, the constraints, the schema version). Help texts and descriptions do not count. The deploy stops with:

ERROR: this git change gives access that has not been approved (skeleton <git> over the accepted <accepted>):
  <role>: <n> new: route iam GET /api/… ; …
  anonymous and services: public monitor GET /api/… ; …
This change needs a qa-approved skeleton version: put HEAD back at the accepted skeleton, keep the change as a commit on a branch, and run ./apps/iam/apply.sh --propose-skeleton --by <you> --reason "<why>" --from-git <commit>; once qa approves it, check that commit out and run ./apps/iam/apply.sh <version>.
Break-glass (MEDCEA_POLICY_FILE) does not bypass this check: it changes the matrix, never the skeleton.
Nothing was changed.

The network rules count in full: besides each pod's allowed sources, any change to how a source is resolved (the ingress namespace, a proxy's release name, a pod's or a calling pod's selector, the ports a pod carries, a calling pod's only_rpc list, the hosts that skip the shared upstreams) is a change that gives access, and so is any change to a database role name, a service identity's MQTT login or database password variable, or the MQTT Explorer's credential settings. Removing an allowed source, a rule, a hop, a resource group or a role only narrows. A key the gate does not know yet counts as giving access too (developers classify it in apps/iam/compiler/explain.py; tests/test_policy_source.py fails until they do). The refusal names such a change "section <key> changed".

The way forward for such a change: put HEAD back at the accepted skeleton, keep the change as a commit on a branch, and propose that commit as a skeleton version (./apps/iam/apply.sh --propose-skeleton --by <you> --reason "<why>" --from-git <commit>, since slice 4.4); a qa person approves it in the Access Policy. While the proposal waits, the deploying tree stays at the accepted skeleton; a tree that carries it is refused by every deploy, and the health check FAILs "the git skeleton widens: a deploy refuses it (proposed as version N, <status>: put HEAD back at the accepted skeleton; the proposal waits on its branch)". Once it is approved, check its commit out and run ./apps/iam/apply.sh N --by <you> (since slice 4.5): the gate lets through exactly the approved skeleton, and only when HEAD contains the proposal's commit; the refusal then reads "This skeleton is approved as version N: run ./apps/iam/apply.sh N --by <you> to apply it (deploys refuse it until then)".

Keep the skeleton commit on the deployed branch. Once skeleton version N is applied, the accepted skeleton is that commit's. A checkout that drops it (an older branch, a reset) is a narrowing to the next deploy, which accepts it without asking: the approved access is silently gone. To undo an applied skeleton version on purpose, git revert the skeleton change and deploy (the deploy accepts the narrowing and records it), plus --rollback-to for the matrix if needed. A skeleton version is never reverted automatically.

A change that only narrows access, or changes nothing a person can reach, is checked first: the git skeleton with the applied matrix must pass the policy checker, otherwise the deploy refuses "the git skeleton … with the applied matrix fails the checker; it is not accepted and nothing was changed" (fix the change in git).
