When it passes, it is accepted by the next deploy and recorded (skeleton_accepted, with the skeleton it replaced, and skeleton_synced); the health check WARNs "the git skeleton narrows: accepted at the next deploy" until then. A change to the matrix: in git is not refused but has no effect: the matrix comes from the applied version (the health check WARNs "git may lag"). ./apps/iam/apply.sh --status shows the accepted and the git skeleton; developers check a change offline with python3 apps/iam/compiler/cli.py skeleton-gate --against-git HEAD --check.

Policy break-glass

When a deploy must compile another matrix than the applied version's (an emergency, before approvals exist), break-glass names a policy file of your own for one run: MEDCEA_POLICY_FILE=<file> MEDCEA_POLICY_BREAK_GLASS="<reason>" ./apps/<component>/deploy.sh (or ./deploy-infra.sh). Without the reason the deploy refuses ("set MEDCEA_POLICY_BREAK_GLASS=<reason>"). For several components at once, export MEDCEA_POLICY_FILE and run ./deploy-apps.sh [--all] --break-glass "<reason>" (asked once, one event naming every selected component that compiles the policy) or ./install.sh --break-glass "<reason>" (asked once, two events: the infrastructure and the applications). Without --break-glass, deploy-apps.sh and install.sh ignore an exported MEDCEA_POLICY_FILE and say so. ./medcea.sh → Policy → How to use policy break-glass shows the same and runs nothing.

  • Break-glass does not bypass the skeleton gate. A git change that gives access is refused under break-glass too, before anything is recorded.
  • It changes only the matrix and the waivers. The file's skeleton must equal the accepted one, and its rows for iam_policy and iam_users must equal the applied version's: break-glass can never change who approves policy or account changes.
  • The deploy prints the file and the reason and asks you to type the word break-glass at the terminal (deploy-apps.sh/install.sh --break-glass ask once for the whole run); without a terminal it refuses.
  • The file is copied to state/break-glass/<time>-<pid>.yaml; that copy is what is compiled, so editing the original afterwards changes nothing. The copy stays as evidence.
  • Before any compile, the deploy records break_glass_seen in the policy history (the copy's SHA-256, the reason, your OS account, the component) and prints in red "BREAK-GLASS: compiling … recorded as event N".
  • The health check's Access policy version FAILs while it is open. It ends per component: that component's next successful deploy without MEDCEA_POLICY_FILE records break_glass_ended as its last step (a deploy that fails leaves it open). ./deploy-infra.sh (infrastructure and, when enabled, the AI workbench) and ./deploy-apps.sh --all end it everywhere. The onboarding wizard's component ends only on a machine with a user session (its deploy skips otherwise).
  • Write the reason and the decision in your operations log.

Re-rendering only what drifted

Since slice 4.2b (November 2026) each script that deploys something compiled from the access policy has a scoped mode. It compiles its targets, compares each with what the cluster runs, prints one line per target (unchanged, re-rendered, not deployed or deferred) and changes only what differs. A second run therefore prints unchanged everywhere and changes nothing. Use it when the health check's Policy artefacts names a stale target, or after the host file changed; ./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume runs all of them for you. ./medcea.sh → Policy → Re-render the policy artefacts runs them in one lock.

CommandTargetsOn a drift
./deploy-infra.sh --policy-onlyThe route table and MQTT rows (ConfigMap medcea-iam-lib), the application pods' network policies, Node-RED's editor rights, Grafana's roles, pgAdmin's sign-in roles, the Node-RED and portal gatesRe-renders that target only. iam-api restarts only when the MQTT rows changed, and the MQTT Explorer credentials issued under the old rows end, as in a full deploy. Grafana and pgAdmin redeploy their whole section (they restart; pgAdmin's sessions end), and only for pgAdmin is Keycloak asked who gets the database entry. Logs to logs/deploy-infra-policy-<time>.log.
./infra/deploy-workbench.sh --policy-onlyThe AI workbench's gate (who may sign in, hub administrators, the refusal message) and the notebooks' network hopsThe same Helm upgrade as a full deploy; the hub restarts only because its values changed. The example notebooks are not touched.
./apps/<c>/deploy.sh --gate-only for frontend, scheduler, monitor, mqtt-explorer, accessThe sign-in gate of that application's host(s): the roles it admits and its 403 pageA Helm upgrade of that proxy only; it rolls by itself because its configuration changed. No other part of the application is touched and nothing is restarted. The User Manager's gate widens only after every access pod proves it enforces, as in a full deploy; without the proof it stays admin-only and the command fails.
./apps/iam/deploy.sh --gate-onlyThe Policy UI's gate (since slice 4.3)A Helm upgrade of iam-oauth2-proxy, proof-gated like the User Manager's.
./apps/edge-wizard/deploy.sh --gate-onlyThe roles the onboarding wizard admits (its --required-role)Restarts the wizard service, which compiles them when it starts. While an onboarding run is in progress it does not restart (that would kill the run): it prints deferred and exits 4. Run ./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume --by <you> after the run has finished.
./apps/superset/deploy.sh --gate-onlySuperset's role mapping (since Superset stage C)Rewrites Secret superset-secrets and ConfigMap superset-config and restarts Superset, which installs its packages from the wheel cache; it also counts a pod started with an older Secret as drift. Stops Superset when the policy no longer gives a role a setting. While the wheel cache is incomplete it prints deferred and exits 4 if the running Superset admits only what the policy still gives, and stops it otherwise (see Superset).

None of these touches Keycloak's realm, the database (except ending outdated MQTT credentials, as above), the TLS certificates or DNS, and none restarts an application, except two gates that are read only at start: the onboarding wizard's (./apps/edge-wizard/deploy.sh --gate-only restarts the cea-edge-wizard service on drift) and Superset's (its --gate-only restarts Superset). The database grants have no scoped mode: ./apps/database/deploy.sh applies them.

The deploy scripts refuse an option they do not know (exit 2, nothing runs). Before 4.2b a mistyped option such as ./deploy-infra.sh --polcy-only ran a full deploy.

apply.sh

./apps/iam/apply.sh applies policy versions. As of slice 4.5 it has these modes; it logs to logs/apply-policy-<time>.log:

CommandWhat it doesLock
--bootstrap --by <username>Version 1 from the factory file, only while no version exists. The iam deploy runs it; by hand only when that waited. Asks you to type yes (a permanent record).yes
--bootstrap --check-only --by <username>Would version 1 bootstrap? Writes nothing.no
--resume --by <username>Finishes an apply that was committed but did not record its end, or one with a deferred target: rewrites the host file, runs every scoped mode under its lock (each re-renders only what drifted), checks the grants, records the end. A target that had to wait (the onboarding wizard during an onboarding run) is recorded as apply_deferred after the end; the health check's Access policy version WARNs until a later --resume re-renders it. The iam deploy runs --resume itself when it finds an unfinished apply. Asks [y/N].yes
--statusThe applied version (who it is claimed by, whether qa confirmed it), open versions, the last policy events, the accepted and git skeleton, the host file, the live digests, open break-glass, recorded and queued account facts.no
--propose-skeleton --by <username> --reason "<text>" --from-git <rev> [--check-only]Since slice 4.4. Proposes the skeleton of commit <rev> (--from-git is mandatory: the deploying tree stays at the accepted skeleton) as a submitted version of kind skeleton, for a qa person's approval in the Access Policy. Only a skeleton that widens access and passes the checker with the applied matrix is proposed ("nothing to approve" otherwise), never under break-glass, never while another change or skeleton version is open. --by is resolved in Keycloak and recorded as the proposer (a claim); the --by username and your OS user are appended to the reason. It prints what each role gains, the digests, and which roles a qa approver may not approve for; asks [y/N]; writes the version and its diff in one transaction (system:apply). Nothing is applied. --check-only writes nothing and takes no lock.yes
--withdraw-open --by <username> --reason "<text>" [--check-only]Since slice 4.4. Withdraws the one open change or skeleton version (draft, submitted or approved) from the host, when the Access Policy cannot (a rollback of 4.4, an aborted test). Shows the version and its authors and asks [y/N]; "nothing is open" exits 0. --by is not looked up in Keycloak (withdrawing grants nothing); it and your OS user are appended to the reason. The withdrawn event names system:apply.yes
<N> --by <username> [--check-only]Since slice 4.5. Applies change or skeleton version N, approved by a qa person in the Access Policy, from a committed tree (uncommitted changes in apps/iam are refused). Before anything changes it checks, and refuses with the reason: the version is approved and based on the applied one, the last apply finished, no open break-glass, the history chain; the approval's token is a realm signature with the expected claims (verified against the key Keycloak publishes now), never reused; the approver is still an enabled account with an approver role, the same person, none of the authors, and no enabled admin account is that person (I17); the version widens no role held by any enabled account of the approver's person; no account decision waits for qa; the recomputed diff is byte for byte the one approved; the version passes the checker. It prints the diff summary (each changed target, hosts' admitted roles before → after, what each role gains or loses), runs the nine artefact checks as a baseline (eight before Superset stage C added Superset roles; any FAIL refuses: fix it first), asks [y/N], reads Keycloak and the version again, then commits the version with its grants compiled from it in one transaction, rewrites the host file, runs every scoped mode and the nine checks again. --check-only stops before the question and writes nothing.yes
--rollback-to <K> --by <username> --reason "<text>" [--check-only]Since slice 4.5. Restores superseded version K (confirmed by qa, not disputed; a change or skeleton version with its approval evidence) as a new version of kind rollback, applied at once and confirmed afterwards by a qa person other than you in the Access Policy. Refused when K's rows under today's skeleton would give any role more than K was approved for ("draft from version K in the Policy UI … and have qa approve it"); rows naming a group or role the skeleton retired are dropped and counted. An open change or skeleton version is withdrawn; pending account decisions are listed, not refused; a check already failing is reported and never drives a revert. Asks you to type yes.yes
--audit <N>Since slice 4.5. Read-only: recompiles version N with the compiler of its recorded commit from its rows, runs the checker, verifies its approval token against the key recorded at apply, and compares every artefact digest with its applied record (cli.py audit-version); exit 1 on a mismatch, 2 when the record cannot be reproduced (for example a commit no longer in the repository).no

--by is your Keycloak username in the realm: it is recorded as the person who applied the version (a claim), and a qa person other than you confirms the version in the Policy UI once it exists (IAM 4.3). Exit codes: 0 done; 1 refused or failed, nothing changed, or (since 4.5) a failed rollout fully reverted; 2 a usage error or a precondition (the bootstrap waits: no migration 008c, Keycloak down, an unknown --by; for N also a check already failing, a narrowing git skeleton, a commit that cannot be reproduced); 3 committed but not finished: run --resume (never for --propose-skeleton or --withdraw-open, after whose commit nothing follows); 130 interrupted before the commit, nothing changed.

When the rollout fails (since 4.5). After the commit every scoped mode runs, then the nine checks; a failed command (or a check FAILing that did not FAIL in the baseline) is retried with every later one, up to 3 attempts 20 s apart. After ./deploy-infra.sh --policy-only apply.sh waits up to 150 s until every Ready pod of the services that check routes reads the new route table; access-api may answer 503 to account decisions for about a minute after the commit when the version moves a role's widening (the summary says so). A change or rollback version still failing after the third attempt is reverted: a second transaction puts the previous version back and files partial_apply {reverting} under it, its artefacts are re-rendered, then partial_apply {reverted} is recorded under N (approved again) and applied {reverted_from} under the previous version; exit 1, "Fix the cause and run … again". What a revert does not undo: retired MQTT person credentials stay retired, pgAdmin lost its sessions if its sign-in roles changed, and narrowings access-api applied in the window stay applied (the health check WARNs until qa reviews them). A skeleton version is not reverted: partial_apply {mixed}, exit 3. Every unfinished state (apply_started, partial_apply mixed or reverting) FAILs the health check and is finished with ./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume --by <you>, which converges forward and never reverts; the iam deploy resumes apply_started itself and only WARNs on partial_apply ("version N ended in partial_apply: ./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume --by <you>"), which wants a person to look. MEDCEA_CONFIRMED=1 skips its own question when the caller has asked already (the iam deploy and medcea.sh do).

One deploy at a time

Every script that changes the cluster or config.env takes the deploy lock first: install.sh, deploy-infra.sh, infra/configure.sh, deploy-apps.sh, each apps/<component>/deploy.sh and uninstall.sh, infra/deploy-workbench.sh, apps/iam/units.sh, tests/iam-signin.sh and the other test scripts that create things, and medcea.sh for the length of a switch recipe. health-check.sh, the read-only tests and every --help do not take it. Two deploys side by side would interleave Helm releases, Keycloak clients and rewrites of config.env.

The lock is held by the kernel on the file .medcea.lock in the repository root. It is released the moment the holding process ends, even after kill -9 or a closed terminal, so there is never a stale lock to delete. A script started by another script that holds the lock (for example install.sh running deploy-infra.sh) uses its parent's lock.

Reading a refusal

A refused script prints Another MedCEA deploy is already running: and exits with code 1. What follows tells you who holds it:

  • A running deploy: its PID, start time, terminal and command, then Wait for it to finish, or stop it with: kill -- -<pgid>. Use that group kill, not a plain kill <pid>: a helm --wait or rollout status the run is waiting on would survive and keep the lock.
  • Leftover processes: The run that started it has ended; these leftover processes still hold the lock, with each process and the kill command to stop them.
  • A run as another user, usually under sudo: the holder could not be inspected, and the message suggests sudo fuser -v on the lock file.

medcea.sh reports a held lock without exiting: it says another deploy is running and returns you to the menu with nothing changed.

medcea.sh, the MedCEA menus

./medcea.sh walks you through the platform's commands by question and answer. It is the recommended way to run anything you do not run every day, and the only supported way to change an IAM switch.

The name. Until 9 November 2026 this was ./guide.sh. It is named after the platform, MedCEA, not after your installation's project name: an install whose PROJECT_NAME is something else still runs ./medcea.sh. The old name still works for now: ./guide.sh prints "guide.sh is now ./medcea.sh (this name will be removed in a later release)" and runs ./medcea.sh with the same options. Change scripts, notes and habits to ./medcea.sh: the old name will be removed in a later release.

  1. Run ./medcea.sh, or ./medcea.sh --dry-run to see what it would do without running or changing anything. Every question and confirmation is still asked in a dry run.
  2. Pick an area: Install and uninstall; Infrastructure; Applications; Operators and units; IAM switches (enable or roll back one switch, or bring every switch still off to full enforcement); Health and tests; Edge devices; Policy (read-only views; the IAM 4.1 and 4.2a deploys; policy versions: status, would version 1 bootstrap, bootstrap by hand, finish an interrupted apply, print the applied policy; how to use policy break-glass, shown and never run); Backups.
  3. Pick an action and answer its questions. Answers are checked the way the target script checks them (unit codes, usernames, component names that exist on disk), and nothing you type may start with -, so an answer cannot turn into an option.
  4. Read the plan: the exact command, whether it is read-only, changes the platform or is destructive, what it changes, whether it takes the deploy lock, and whether it needs sudo.
  5. Confirm. A read-only command asks [Y/n]; a change asks [y/N]; a destructive one (an uninstall, --purge-data, --reset, --bootstrap, erasing a board) wants the word yes typed in full, and --purge-data also the project name.
  6. The command runs in your terminal, so its own prompts work, and medcea.sh reports its exit code.
  7. At a terminal these steps are dialog boxes (see Dialog boxes and the status header); ./medcea.sh --plain keeps the numbered questions.

medcea.sh never asks for a password or secret: the commands it runs ask for their own. Ctrl+D (end of input) leaves medcea.sh. For units and policy commands it asks for --by, your own Keycloak username, and offers your last answer as the default for the rest of the session.

Dialog boxes and the status header

Since 9 November 2026, when you start medcea.sh at a terminal, its menus and questions are dialog boxes (whiptail) instead of numbered lists. The questions, the checks on your answers, the plan and the commands are the same as in the numbered mode; only the way you answer changes.

  • Menus. Each menu lists its entries with the same numbers as the numbered mode, as "label — purpose" (a long purpose is cut with …). Move with the arrow keys (or Page Up and Page Down), press Enter on Select. Tab moves between the list and the buttons. Back (or Esc) returns to the menu above; on the first menu the button is Quit.
  • Questions. A question you type is an input box, with the default already filled in (for example your --by username after the first time). An empty answer (Enter on OK) is the same as in the numbered mode: an optional question takes its default, a required one comes back with the reason it was refused shown above it, exactly as when a typed answer is refused. Cancel or Esc is not an answer: it leaves the action, nothing is run, and the menu comes back with "Cancelled; nothing was run." (a remembered --by stays remembered). A yes/no question has Yes and No buttons; the one the numbered mode would take on Enter is selected, and Esc is No.
  • The plan and its confirmation. The plan (command, kind, what it changes, the deploy lock, sudo, notes) is the text of the confirmation box. A read-only command has Yes selected; a change has No selected, so Enter alone cancels; a destructive command opens a box titled DESTRUCTIVE in which you type yes (and, for --purge-data, then the project name in a second box). A dry run ends in a box with the line "[dry run] not executed: …".
  • Running. The command does not run in a box: the screen is cleared, medcea.sh prints what it said since the last box and the $ command line, and the command runs in your terminal as before, in colour, with its own questions, sudo password prompts and output. Then medcea.sh prints "Finished" or "Failed" with the exit code.
  • When the command has ended. A box titled Finished: exit code 0 or Failed: exit code N sums it up: the command line and its result, the log file it wrote in logs/ (when it wrote one: open that file for the whole output), what medcea.sh said afterwards, and the last lines of the command's output (about 300, colours removed; scroll with the arrow keys or Page Up and Page Down after Tab). Menu (or Esc) returns to the menu, Quit leaves medcea.sh. A switch recipe or Bring IAM to full enforcement shows one such box when it has ended, with a line for each command it ran (when Bring IAM to full enforcement stops before its end although every command it ran passed, for example at a checklist answered No, the box is titled Stopped: full enforcement not finished, or Not finished: the apps were not redeployed when you declined the last redeploy, never Finished), and in between asks you to press Enter before any question box, so you can read the output first. To show the box, medcea.sh runs the command under script (part of util-linux, on every Ubuntu host), which copies what the command writes into a private file (mode 600, in medcea.sh's own folder, mode 700) and is deleted as soon as the box is built: it is never kept or copied. When a command's output holds the credentials box (./install.sh, a standalone ./deploy-infra.sh), there is no summary box: the credentials stay on the terminal, medcea.sh says why, and Enter returns to the menu (q then Enter leaves). Without script it is the same prompt after every command.
  • Leaving. Quit on the first menu or in the box after a command. Ctrl+C does nothing while a box is on the screen (use Esc); while a command runs it stops the command (and only the command: the box then says Failed: exit code 130), and in a recipe it stops the recipe as described below. Whatever medcea.sh had not shown yet (an error, "Bye.") is printed on the terminal when it ends. If a box fails (whiptail cannot open the terminal or is killed), medcea.sh ends with "the dialog box failed (whiptail exit N …): run ./medcea.sh --plain" and exit code 1, puts the terminal mode back as it was at the start and runs nothing; at a question of Bring IAM to full enforcement it stops the chain as Ctrl+C there does.

The MedCEA logo. On a large terminal (about 32 lines and 75 columns or more) the first menu shows the MedCEA logo above the status header: the herb, the MedCEA lettering with "Controlled Environment Agriculture for Medicinal Plants and Fungi", and the mushroom. When there is not room for the logo, the whole header and every area, it is left out; the menus below the first never show it. In the numbered mode the coloured logo is printed once at the start (only on a terminal); ./deploy-infra.sh prints the same logo when a deploy starts.

Every menu starts with a status header. It only reads files on the host: it never contacts the cluster or the database and never takes the deploy lock.

LineWhat it shows
Host, KernelThe host name and the running kernel (uname -r). They are also on the line above the box, with the commit.
GitThe branch and short commit of the repository medcea.sh runs from, and dirty when git status shows changed or untracked files; "not a git checkout" otherwise.
HealthThe summary line of the newest health check log (logs/health-check-*.log), for example "63 OK, 1 warning(s), 0 failures — 64 checks", and how long ago it ran. It is the last run's result, not a new check: run Health and tests → Health check for a fresh one.
PolicyThe applied policy version on this host, from the first line of state/policy-applied.yaml, as version=N kind=K; none applied on this host before version 1; unreadable when the file or state/ cannot be read.
LockWhether the lock is held is read from the kernel's list of locks (/proc/locks), without taking it. held by <command> (pid N) when it is held and the run named in .medcea.lock has the file open; held, not by the run its file names (ended) when a process that run left (a helm --wait after a plain kill) still holds it: find it with fuser -v .medcea.lock; held: its last taker, pid N (…), is another user's process for a run under sudo, whose files medcea.sh cannot see; otherwise free, whatever PID the file names (an old run's PID may belong to another process by now).
DRY RUNShown under --dry-run: nothing is run and config.env is not changed.

The numbered mode is still there: ./medcea.sh --plain (or MEDCEA_PLAIN=1 ./medcea.sh; GUIDE_PLAIN=1, its old name, still works) uses it at a terminal too, and medcea.sh uses it by itself when its input or output is piped, when whiptail is not installed, when the terminal type is unknown (TERM empty or dumb), when the terminal is not the session's controlling terminal (/dev/tty cannot be opened, for example under setsid) and when it is smaller than 44 columns by 18 lines (the boxes would hide the status header); the last two print why at the start. A menu keeps the whole status header on screen: its list gets fewer rows (it scrolls) before the header is cut. The boxes use a dark colour scheme unless you set NEWT_COLORS yourself.

Switch recipes

For an IAM switch or WORKBENCH_ENABLED, medcea.sh shows the switch's current value, then the recipe for enabling it or rolling it back:

  • Before you start: a checklist of preconditions, which you confirm once. medcea.sh does not test the checklist items for you. Some preconditions it does check itself and refuses the recipe with the reason (for example, enabling IAM_DB_ROLES while IAM_POSTGREST_JWT is not true).
  • Steps, in order: each is either a change to one line of config.env or a command. The recipe takes the deploy lock once for all its steps and stops at the first step that fails, or at Ctrl+C.
  • Notes: what happens afterwards and how to check it.

The switch must be on exactly one active line in config.env; with none or several, medcea.sh refuses and says which lines to fix. A switch that another recipe's order depends on (IAM_DB_ROLES, IAM_POSTGREST_JWT, IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES) must be written literally as "true" or "false".

Before the first change, medcea.sh copies config.env to config.env.guide-<timestamp>.bak (mode 600, not in git). It shows only the changed line, never the lines around it, which may be passwords. If a step fails, it tells you whether config.env was already changed and prints the cp -p command that puts the backup back. Restoring the file does not undo the steps that already ran; each step is safe to repeat, so the usual fix is to correct the cause and run the recipe again. After a recipe completes, medcea.sh offers to delete the backup, because it is a full copy with every password. ./install.sh --uninstall-all deletes any backups that are left.

IAM switches → Bring IAM to full enforcement runs the enable recipe of every IAM switch still false, in order, under one lock, and stops at the first problem; running it again resumes. See After a fresh install.

The IAM switches

The access controls (IAM) were built in phases. Each phase has a switch in config.env, turned on in order with a recipe in ./medcea.sh (IAM switches). A fresh install has the first two and IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES on and the rest off (see After a fresh install). Each one can be rolled back the same way.

SwitchWhen trueValue on the install of 31 October 2026
IAM_GATESEach sign-in gate, Grafana's own role setting, the AI workbench's sign-in, the device onboarding wizard and pgAdmin admit only the roles the access policy compiles for their host. False puts every gate back on the list used before the access policy (operator, qa, auditor, admin), except Node-RED and the MQTT Explorer, which keep engineer and Node-RED's editor rights from the policy; the User Manager on admin only, Grafana on any enabled account (at least Viewer) and the AI workbench on any enabled account, with ADMIN_USER as hub administrator; device onboarding goes back to EDGE_WIZARD_ROLE (empty: any signed-in account), and pgAdmin stays admin only.true
IAM_NETPOLOne network policy per application pod: only its listed callers can connect; anything else times out.true
IAM_POSTGREST_JWTconfig-api (PostgREST, behind the System Configuration UI and the onboarding wizard) verifies the person's sign-in token.true
IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLESEach database client (scheduler, monitor, Database Management, Node-RED, Grafana, pgAdmin, and since IAM 3.5 iam-api, since 8 November 2026 Superset) logs in as its own database role instead of the superuser. Superset and iam-api are not deployed while it is false: they never log in as the superuser.true
IAM_DB_ROLESThe database enforces per-role grants, row-level security and guard triggers, including the operator's unit and assigned-run checks.true
IAM_ENFORCEThe five Python services (scheduler, monitor, Database Management, the Config UI's platform API, the User Manager) refuse what the route table does not allow. False: they only log medcea_iam: would refuse … and let the request through.true (since 31 October 2026)
IAM_MQTT_PERSONThe MQTT Explorer connects with a short-lived credential of each person's own, made from their role and accepted only on the broker's WebSocket listener; False: one sign-in check for both broker listeners (services and boards), and the Explorer has no credential: its page says it needs this switch. The shared mqtt-explorer account is gone in both cases (removed 1 November 2026; see MQTT Explorer).true (since 31 October 2026, IAM 3.5)
WORKBENCH_ENABLEDdeploy-infra.sh also deploys the AI workbench (JupyterHub, about 2 GB of images).true

The values above are those in config.env on 31 October 2026, on the install that ran before any reinstall. IAM 2.6 first ran in report-only mode; IAM_ENFORCE was turned on that day, followed by ./deploy-infra.sh and ./deploy-apps.sh --all, and IAM_MQTT_PERSON, the last switch, after the Phase 3 deploy. A fresh install does not start there: it has only the first two switches and IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES on until Bring IAM to full enforcement has run (see After a fresh install). Always read the current value in ./medcea.sh, which shows it from config.env before offering a recipe.

Two parts enforce whatever IAM_ENFORCE says: the User Manager's admin port and Database Management. They have no off switch.

Order and prerequisites

  1. IAM_GATES and IAM_NETPOL stand on their own. For IAM_NETPOL, every caller of an application pod must be listed under network: in apps/iam/policy/defaults.yaml.
  2. IAM_POSTGREST_JWT needs AUTHENTICATOR_DB_PASS set and different from POSTGRES_PASS (configuration generates it).
  3. IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES, then check that the health check shows dbclients OK. A new install starts with it on (since 8 November 2026).
  4. IAM_DB_ROLES: medcea.sh refuses it until IAM_POSTGREST_JWT and IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES are both true, and the database deploy refuses it, changing nothing, until every database client has moved to its own role. Before it, every operator needs a unit in effect, confirmed by qa (see Operators and units); an operator without one sees no telemetry or runs and starts none.
  5. IAM_MQTT_PERSON needs ./apps/iam/deploy.sh to have run (it deploys iam-api, which issues the credentials and logs in to the database only as its own role, so IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES must be true), ./apps/access/deploy.sh since the IAM 3.5 pull (a fresh install's ./install.sh has run it), and IAM_DB_ROLES true (the broker reads the credentials through its compiled grants). Until it is true the MQTT Explorer has no credential (there is no shared account any more).
  6. IAM_ENFORCE needs IAM_DB_ROLES true: only the database checks that an operator's run belongs to their unit. medcea.sh lists this in its checklist but does not refuse; the health check reports iamenforce FAIL while IAM_ENFORCE is true and IAM_DB_ROLES false. It should follow a report-only trial in which every "would refuse" line from a real person is intended policy, because each becomes a refusal.

Recipes

./medcea.sh runs these steps for you. They are listed here so you know what each recipe does.

SwitchEnableRoll back
IAM_GATESset true; ./deploy-infra.sh; ./deploy-apps.sh --all. Check with tests/iam-hosts.sh and tests/iam-workbench.sh.IAM_GATES=false ./apps/access/deploy.sh (narrows the User Manager first); set false; ./deploy-infra.sh; ./deploy-apps.sh --all. Node-RED and the MQTT Explorer keep their gate (engineer). Accounts with production_manager, maintenance, qc, qp, engineer, bio_scientist or control_scientist lose the portal and every other gated host until it is true again. Grafana admits any enabled account again; its old grafana_* roles are re-created, so Editor and Admin go only to the old built-in accounts that still exist. The AI workbench admits any enabled account again; its hub administrator still cannot open others' workspaces, and removing a person from the hub still keeps their files.
IAM_NETPOLset true; ./deploy-infra.sh. Check with tests/iam-network.sh; the health check iamnetpol compares the policies' names with the compile.set false; ./deploy-infra.sh. At once, without a deploy: microk8s kubectl -n <namespace> delete netpol -l medcea/iam-netpol=true (until the next deploy-infra.sh while it is still true).
IAM_POSTGREST_JWT./deploy-infra.sh; set true; ./apps/frontend/deploy.sh.If IAM_DB_ROLES is true, first set it false, run ./infra/deploy-workbench.sh and ./apps/database/deploy.sh; then set false and run ./apps/frontend/deploy.sh. The frontend deploy also closes the AI workbench notebooks' route to config-api if it is still open.
IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLESset true; ./deploy-apps.sh --all; ./deploy-infra.sh. Check dbclients OK.Refused while IAM_DB_ROLES is true. Set false; ./deploy-apps.sh --all; ./deploy-infra.sh; ./apps/database/deploy.sh (the last makes the service roles unable to log in again).
IAM_DB_ROLESset true; ./apps/database/deploy.sh (it restarts config-api itself); ./infra/deploy-workbench.sh, which opens the AI workbench notebooks' route to config-api and Keycloak now that config-api and the database have both switched.set false; ./infra/deploy-workbench.sh (closes the notebooks' route first); ./apps/database/deploy.sh, which also closes the route on a running workbench before the database changes, so no notebook reaches config-api while the older, wider grants are back. While IAM_ENFORCE is true, roll that back too unless the rollback is brief.
IAM_ENFORCEpython3 tests/iam-routes-diff.py --strict; set true; ./deploy-infra.sh.set false; ./deploy-infra.sh.
IAM_MQTT_PERSONWith no run active: set true; ./apps/iam/deploy.sh (it refuses if iam-api cannot run yet, before anything else changes); ./deploy-infra.sh (restarts the broker; the boards reconnect within seconds); ./apps/mqtt-explorer/deploy.sh (it waits until iam-api has read the switch, about a minute). Engineers then reload the Explorer. Check with ./health-check.sh (MQTT person credentials) and tests/iam-mqtt.sh.set false; ./deploy-infra.sh; ./apps/mqtt-explorer/deploy.sh. Every personal credential is ended (kept in the database, never reused), and the Explorer has no credential until the switch is true again: the shared account does not come back (removed 1 November 2026).
WORKBENCH_ENABLEDset true; ./deploy-infra.sh.set false; ./deploy-infra.sh. This does not remove a workbench already running; later deploys only skip it.

After switching IAM_ENFORCE

The services read the switch on each request from the shared access settings that ./deploy-infra.sh publishes (the medcea-iam-lib ConfigMap), so the change is live within about a minute with no restart. From then on a refused request is answered 401 (no token or a bad one), 403 (the route or role is not allowed) or 503 (the service cannot verify tokens). Each application pod also keeps a copy of the switch from its last deploy, used only if the route-table mount is missing; it stays at the old value until the app is deployed again, and the health check reports iamenforce as FAIL until then. Redeploy the apps with ./deploy-apps.sh --all when no recipe run is active (Bring IAM to full enforcement asks for this at its end). Then check with tests/iam-check.sh, ./health-check.sh and tests/iam-signin.sh.

A rollback of IAM_ENFORCE returns the services to logging "would refuse" within about a minute.

When IAM_MQTT_PERSON changes, ./deploy-infra.sh appends enforcement_enabled or enforcement_disabled with {switch: IAM_MQTT_PERSON} to the same history, and every credential the Explorer is given is an mqtt_credential_issued event naming the person, the role, the topics and the expiry (never the password). On every switch change, and whenever the MQTT part of the access policy has changed, ./deploy-infra.sh ends the credentials issued before it and records mqtt_credentials_retired with their number; open Explorer pages then ask for a new credential.

When IAM_ENFORCE or IAM_DB_ROLES changes, the deploy appends an enforcement_enabled or enforcement_disabled event to the access policy history, a hash chain in the database that the health check verifies. For IAM_ENFORCE the event carries {switch: IAM_ENFORCE}. Each ./deploy-infra.sh also writes the current values of IAM_GATES, IAM_NETPOL and IAM_POSTGREST_JWT into the route-table settings with the time, which the quarterly access review records.

A git revert of IAM code comes only after the switch is rolled back. A reverted deploy breaks a config-api that is still in token mode, and reverting the database phase also needs a manual database step, which medcea.sh's IAM_DB_ROLES rollback notes name.

After a fresh install

Every new config.env is made from config.env.example, and neither ./install.sh nor the setup questions change the IAM switches. A fresh install therefore comes up with the sign-in gates, the network policies and (since 8 November 2026) the services' own database roles on, but without token checks at config-api, database role enforcement, row-level security or service enforcement:

SwitchFresh installWhat it does when true
IAM_GATEStrueEach sign-in gate, Grafana, the AI workbench, the onboarding wizard and pgAdmin admit the roles the access policy compiles for them.
IAM_NETPOLtrueOnly each application pod's listed callers can connect to it.
IAM_POSTGREST_JWTfalseconfig-api verifies the person's sign-in token.
IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLEStrue (since 8 November 2026; false before)Each database client logs in as its own role instead of the superuser; Superset and iam-api are installed.
IAM_DB_ROLESfalseThe database enforces per-role grants, row-level security and guard triggers, including an operator's units.
IAM_ENFORCEfalseThe Python services refuse what the route table does not allow, instead of logging "would refuse".
IAM_MQTT_PERSONfalseThe MQTT Explorer uses a personal, short-lived credential. While false, the Explorer has no credential at all (the shared account was removed on 1 November 2026).

The health check warns while IAM_POSTGREST_JWT, IAM_DB_ROLES, IAM_ENFORCE, IAM_MQTT_PERSON or IAM_GATES is off, so a fresh install never prints "All checks passed". It does not warn for the other two: dbclients is OK when every client logs in as the switch says (each on its own role while IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is on, every one on postgres while it is off), and iamnetpol WARNs while IAM_NETPOL is off (since 9 November 2026; before, no check read it). That is deliberate: each switch has its own rollback, and an administrator turns them on in order. Some cannot be on at the very first install:

  • IAM_DB_ROLES needs the scheduler and Node-RED already deployed and logging in to the database as their own roles (IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES). On a fresh install the database is deployed before them, so its deploy would refuse.
  • Operators need units assigned and confirmed by a qa person before IAM_DB_ROLES, or they see no telemetry or runs and start none (see Operators and units).

The services' own database roles from the start

Since 8 November 2026 a new config.env has IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES="true", so that Superset, whose data connection is never the database superuser, installs with everything else (decision "Superset installed by default" in the decision record). What that means on a fresh install:

  • ./install.sh runs ./deploy-infra.sh a second time after the applications, so Grafana and pgAdmin move onto svc_grafana and rr_admin_login; afterwards dbclients is OK.
  • pgAdmin holds rr_admin's grants only: it can change no table structure and write no data. For those, use psql in the PostgreSQL pod.
  • The scheduler's log settings become proposals that a qa person approves in the Configuration UI's Approvals tab, which reaches the database through config-api; until IAM_POSTGREST_JWT is on, config-api serves every request as anonymous and the approval is refused, so a proposal waits.
  • iam-api and the Access Policy are deployed; confirming version 1 and approving versions there answer "need IAM_POSTGREST_JWT=true and IAM_DB_ROLES=true" (503) until both are on.
  • Superset is installed when the iam deploy has applied version 1. Its first install downloads three packages from pypi.org (from a pod), besides the images every install pulls; a firewall that blocks PyPI stops it there.

An install that keeps an older config.env (a reinstall that kept it, or an install from before that date) keeps its value: with "false" the infrastructure runs once, Superset is skipped and the install ends with "Still to do: Superset was skipped, it needs IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES=true." A config.env with no line for the switch (from before Phase 2.5) is given "false" by the setup, which says so once. Turning it on is the owner's choice: ./medcea.sh → IAM switches → IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES, then ./apps/superset/deploy.sh.

The order is: IAM_POSTGREST_JWT; IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES (already on, on a new install); assign the operators' units in the User Manager (or with apps/iam/units.sh assign … --by <your username> on the host) and have a qa person confirm them; IAM_DB_ROLES; IAM_ENFORCE (after a report-only trial, see The IAM switches); IAM_MQTT_PERSON; then, with no recipe run active, ./deploy-apps.sh --all, so every app pod's copy of IAM_ENFORCE is true. Until that redeploy ./health-check.sh reports iamenforce FAIL ("pod IAM_ENFORCE copy still false"); after it the IAM checks are OK.

Bring IAM to full enforcement

./medcea.sh → IAM switches → Bring IAM to full enforcement runs that order for you. It uses each switch's own enable recipe, the same one the switch's own entry runs, so nothing in it differs from turning the switches on one by one.

  1. It reads every IAM switch from config.env. Each must be on exactly one active line and written literally as "true" or "false"; otherwise it refuses and changes nothing. If every switch is already true, it says so and stops.
  2. It shows the plan: each switch still false, in the order above (IAM_GATES and IAM_NETPOL only if they are false), with its purpose, its checklist, its steps and its notes. You confirm the whole plan once ([y/N]).
  3. It takes the deploy lock once for the whole chain (refused while another deploy runs), then runs the switches in turn. For each, it asks that switch's checklist when its turn comes, because some items only become true after the switches before it.
  4. Before IAM_DB_ROLES it runs apps/iam/units.sh list under its lock. If an enabled operator has no unit in effect, or the list cannot be read, it says what that means and asks whether to go on; answering no stops the chain there.
  5. Each switch's steps run as in its own recipe: one line of config.env changed, with its own backup, and the deploys in order.
  6. When IAM_ENFORCE was one of the switches, it then asks "No run is active: redeploy the apps now?" ([y/N]) and, on yes, runs ./deploy-apps.sh --all under the same lock, so every app pod carries IAM_ENFORCE="true". On a fresh install no run is active: answer yes. If you answer no, or the redeploy fails, it says that every switch is true but the apps are still to be redeployed, and ./health-check.sh reports iamenforce FAIL until you run ./deploy-apps.sh --all.

On a fresh install, expect a run made soon after the install to stop at IAM_ENFORCE's checklist, whose first item is that a report-only trial is over. Answer no unless the services have already run long enough with "would refuse" lines that are all intended (the trial needs no other switch, so it can run while you work through the earlier ones). Then run the trial (see The IAM switches) and choose the action again: it resumes from IAM_ENFORCE and goes on to IAM_MQTT_PERSON. In the same way, if the operators' units are not yet assigned and confirmed by a qa person, answer no at the question before IAM_DB_ROLES, assign them, and choose the action again.

It stops at the first refused checklist, failed step or Ctrl+C (exit code 130). Ctrl+C while it waits at a question stops it at once, before any step of that switch; during a step it stops once that step's command has ended. It then says which switch stopped and why, which switches are already done, which were not started, and the backups it made. Fix the cause and choose Bring IAM to full enforcement again: switches already true are skipped, so it resumes from the one that stopped. If that switch's own line was already set to true before its steps failed, put its backup back first, using the cp -p command medcea.sh prints (only that switch changes back), or finish it with its own entry in IAM switches. Do not put back an earlier backup: it would turn off switches whose deploys already ran. After a complete chain medcea.sh offers to delete the backups.

./medcea.sh --dry-run shows the plan and every command and config.env change, without running anything, changing anything or taking the lock.

The health check

./health-check.sh checks every service and IAM control listed in health-checks.conf and prints one line per check. It is read-only and does not take the deploy lock. Options: --verbose shows detail for passing checks too, --timeout SECS sets the per-check timeout (default 8), --config FILE reads another check list.

ResultMeaning
OKThe check passed.
WARNNot broken, but not in its final state: for example a switch still false, a pod's copy of a setting that is out of date, or a decision waiting a long time.
FAILSomething is wrong or disagrees with config.env. The message names the cause and usually the command that fixes it.
SKIPThe check does not apply yet (for example the component it reads is not installed).

The summary is All N checks passed., or a count of OK, warnings and failures. The script exits 1 if any check failed. Services that are still starting usually pass a minute later.

The checks iamdbroles, postgrest, iamenforce and iammqtt WARN on purpose while their switch is false, so a platform that is not fully enforcing never prints "All checks passed". grafanarole, iamworkbench, onboardroles and pgadminroles WARN while IAM_GATES is false; iamnetpol WARNs while IAM_NETPOL is false. The proxies' gates are compared by iamartefacts; that a gate admits and refuses as compiled, and that a network policy really drops a connection, are tested with tests/iam-hosts.sh and tests/iam-network.sh. On the install of 31 October 2026 every switch was true, IAM_MQTT_PERSON included, and the health check passed all 50 checks it had that evening (52 before IAM 4.2a, 54 after it, 55 with the Platform manual check of 3 November 2026; see the manual in the portal; 56 with Superset roles of 6 November 2026, which is SKIP until Superset is installed; 57 with Container AppArmor of 8 November 2026, the first check, see the host checks; 61 with the four Phase 5 checks of 9 November 2026, iamloaded, jwks, kcscopes and iamnetpol, see below; 64 with the three of Phase 5's second round, also of 9 November 2026, iamdrift, iamanchor and iamcatalog). A fresh install shows these WARNs until Bring IAM to full enforcement has run, and iamenforce FAIL after it until the apps are redeployed (the chain asks for that at its end).

The IAM checks

Check (type, and the name the output shows)OK whenWARN or FAIL
iamchain (Access policy history)The hash chain of the access policy history verifies.FAIL names the event where the chain is broken. The check reads in a read-only session, as every database check does. WARN when the database's iam_policy.verify_chain() is not SECURITY DEFINER, or the role iam_svc may not execute it: the Policy UI's History tab then cannot verify the chain (run ./apps/database/deploy.sh).
iamanchor (History chain anchor)The access policy history still holds the event the newest complete nightly backup recorded as the chain's head (the line # policy chain head (read before the dump): … of its MANIFEST, see Backup and restore), with the same hash. The text names the event, the backup's age and how many events came since. The history is read in a read-only session; the event number is passed to it as a value, never as SQL. The backup folder is read as backupage reads it, without sudo.FAIL when that event is missing ("the history was cut after that backup (or restored from an older one)"), when its hash differs ("the history was rewritten after that backup"; the message shows the first 12 characters of each hash) or when the table iam_policy.history is gone. After the platform database is restored from a backup older than the newest one this FAILs until the next nightly backup records the restored chain's head (see Restoring). When the newest backup completed before the history's first event was written, it is a backup of an earlier database (BACKUP_DIR is kept across a new install and apps/database/uninstall.sh --purge-data): WARN "no anchor: the newest complete backup … predates this database …" until the next nightly backup, never a comparison of two unrelated chains. WARN when BACKUP_DIR does not exist or cannot be read (run the check as the account that ran ./apps/backup/deploy.sh, which owns the folder, mode 700), when there is no complete backup yet, when the newest one's MANIFEST cannot be read or names no head (a backup from before IAM 4.5) or says the head was unavailable, when the newest complete backup is over 48 hours old, when the chain did not verify at backup time (verify_chain=f), and when the database cannot be read. It does not prove anything against someone with superuser rights in the database and access to the host, who could change both the history and the backup folder.
iamdbroles (Database roles mode)The database records IAM_DB_ROLES=true, as config.env says.WARN while false. FAIL when the database and config.env disagree (run ./apps/database/deploy.sh).
iamcatalog (Database catalog)In the platform database every table, view, sequence, function and schema of medcea, medcea_auth, iam_policy and iam is owned by medcea_owner; every freeze and append-only trigger of the account record (iam), every append-only, no-truncate and retired-recipe guard trigger of medcea and iam_policy, and user_unit_audit_trg and commissioning_history_trg are ENABLE ALWAYS (so a session in replica mode cannot skip them); every view of medcea runs with the reader's rights (security_invoker). The statements are those of tests/iam-db.sh's catalog checks, word for word, run in one read-only session.FAIL on any hit, with the count and the first five object names (names are not secrets): "N object(s) not owned by medcea_owner: …", "… trigger(s) not ENABLE ALWAYS: …", "N medcea view(s) without security_invoker: …". The message names ./apps/database/deploy.sh; see Troubleshooting for what a deploy puts back and what it does not. WARN when the catalog cannot be read; SKIP before ./apps/database/deploy.sh (no role medcea_owner or schema medcea). It notices a protective trigger that was disabled, not one that was dropped: neither this check nor iamgrants (which compares only the iam_ guard triggers of medcea under IAM_DB_ROLES=true) sees a dropped one; tests/iam-db.sh's trigger counts catch it on the test database only.
iamgrants (Database grants)The database's grants equal the compiled policy (checked in a read-only transaction). The text names the set that ran: under IAM_DB_ROLES=true every grantee, row-level security, the triggers and the classification of every table; under false the managed roles and the older set only.FAIL on any drift. Expected right after a pull until ./apps/database/deploy.sh has run. Under IAM_DB_ROLES=false, WARN when a table or view of medcea (also a materialized view, a partitioned or a foreign table) belongs to no resource group ("N medcea object(s) belong to no group …"): give it a member entry in the access policy before the switch, which refuses it. Functions are not classified, by this WARN or by the switch's own check: a new function needs its member entry all the same. SKIP only before the database deploy that adds what the check asks for; drift is never a SKIP (until 9 November 2026 a drift whose detail named a missing function could read as one).
iampolicy (Access policy version)A version of the access policy is applied, state/policy-applied.yaml is exactly that version (its header and its whole body against the database), the skeleton in git adds no access over the accepted one, no earlier accept added any, the last apply recorded its end, no policy break-glass is open, the version audit and the policy history's chain are clean, and no waiver's review date has passed. Before the Policy UI exists (IAM 4.3) it reads "version 1 (bootstrap), qa confirms it in the Policy UI once it exists".FAIL on any of those, naming the command: no version yet ("./apps/iam/deploy.sh bootstraps it"), the host file absent or different (the next deploy rewrites it), a host file without a version (see Policy source), a widening skeleton ("a deploy would refuse it"), an unfinished apply (./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume --by <you>), an open break-glass (the components still to deploy). WARN while an apply runs, while account facts wait in state/seed-facts.jsonl, when the skeleton in git narrows (accepted at the next deploy), when git's matrix lags the applied one (cli.py export-applied), when a waiver's review is due within 30 days, or when a version was rolled back and account decisions applied at once while it was live (pure narrowings) still wait for a qa person's review in the User Manager's Decisions tab (from IAM 4.5, when a rollback exists). It also WARNs when the compiler the Policy UI runs (ConfigMap iam-compiler) is not this checkout's ("the Policy UI compiles with compiler …, this checkout's is …": ./apps/iam/deploy.sh). SKIP before migration 008c. The detail lists every warning and failure. Its applied version is the database's: that the services run that version's route table is iamloaded's proof.
iamartefacts (Policy artefacts)The route table and the MQTT rows in ConfigMap medcea-iam-lib (data and annotations) and the roles each sign-in proxy admits are what the applied version compiles to. Hosts whose proxy is not deployed (the Policy UI's, until IAM 4.3) are counted, not failed.FAIL on a digest or a gate that differs, naming the deploy that writes it. WARN while the User Manager's gate is admin-only (not every access pod has proved it enforces: ./apps/access/deploy.sh). SKIP before ./deploy-infra.sh. Grafana, the AI workbench, Node-RED, the onboarding wizard and pgAdmin keep their own checks.
iamloaded (Policy loaded by services)Every running pod of the six services that check routes (scheduler, monitor, dbmgmt, config-ui, access, iam-api) has loaded the route table the ConfigMap medcea-iam-lib holds: the digest of its /iam/routes.json equals the ConfigMap's medcea/routes-digest. Each pod is read with one read-only kubectl exec that prints only the digest and the applied version. The text lists the applied versions the pods report, for information only: a pod with the current digest and an older applied version is OK (the version number is not part of the digest, and a change that leaves the routes alone does not touch them). Services that are not deployed, or have no running pod, are counted, not failed.FAIL when a pod's digest still differs 120 seconds or more after the ConfigMap's last change ("pod … loads routes …, the ConfigMap holds … since N s", naming that service's deploy script), and when the file is missing or unreadable in a pod of a service that enforces (access, dbmgmt and iam-api always, the others while IAM_ENFORCE is true): it refuses every request. WARN on the same difference within the 120 seconds (the kubelet copies the ConfigMap into the pods within that time), on a missing file where the service does not enforce, and when a pod cannot be read. The 120 seconds are counted from the newest write time Kubernetes records on the ConfigMap (metadata.managedFields, which the check asks kubectl for explicitly), against this host's clock; a time it cannot read counts as past, and the message then says "since an unknown time" rather than an age. SKIP before ./deploy-infra.sh.
iamdecisions (Account decisions)No account decision has waited for qa for over 7 days.WARN on an older waiting decision or a pending mail settings change (User Manager, Decisions tab). FAIL when the access or database deploy is missing a step, naming which to run. SKIP without the access component.
iampending (Changes waiting for qa)No proposed configuration change (unit commissioning, a log setting, the review of a commissioning end) has waited for qa for over 7 days.WARN on an older one, with its number (Configuration UI, Approvals tab). SKIP before the database deploy that adds the approval functions.
iamdrift (Account drift)Keycloak's accounts agree with the account record. The User Manager's service (access-api) compares them in the background every 10 minutes (DRIFT_INTERVAL_SECONDS, 600, never below 60) with its own service account, the same comparison as the red banner in the User Manager's Decisions tab, and publishes only counts and times on its admin port; the check reads them with one read-only kubectl exec into the access pod (no token, no sign-in event, no names). OK reads "N accounts: 0 unexplained roles, 0 failed compensations, 0 enabled while pending, 0 unrecorded; computed S s ago (every 600 s)".FAIL when an account holds a platform role that no confirmed decision, signed-off access review or seed fact explains (the role ./deploy-infra.sh gave an account it created, or first observed on QA_USER/ENGINEER_USER; a fresh install is therefore not red), or when a compensation failed (Keycloak gives more than the record says): User Manager → Decisions. WARN when an account is enabled while its grant or activation still waits for qa; when an enabled account has no access request, decision or status change at all and was not seeded by ./deploy-infra.sh (an account_seeded fact on the policy history): review it in the User Manager and record it (an access request and its decision) or remove it: a signed-off access review does not accept it, only seeded accounts are exempt; when the result is older than 30 minutes, the last computation failed (the kind of error only), Keycloak's list was cut at 10000 accounts, or the seeded accounts could not be read; while a freshly started pod has not computed yet; and when the running access-api predates the drift report ("./apps/access/deploy.sh"). Service accounts are never counted. SKIP without the access component.
dbclients (Database clients)Every deployed database client logs in as the role the switch says.WARN while a client disagrees; deploy it again (Grafana and pgAdmin with ./deploy-infra.sh).
postgrest (PostgREST tokens)config-api runs the token-verifying setup, it was started with the keys the Secret medcea-jwks holds now, and a forged token gets 401. Whether those keys are the realm's is jwks's check (since 9 November 2026).WARN while IAM_POSTGREST_JWT is false. FAIL when config-api runs older keys than the Secret (run ./deploy-infra.sh) or a changed password Secret (run ./apps/frontend/deploy.sh).
grafanarole (Grafana roles)Grafana runs the role setting compiled from the access policy, refuses a role without a setting, and cannot give Grafana Admin through the sign-in.WARN while IAM_GATES is false (any enabled account gets in). FAIL when the running setting differs from the policy (run ./deploy-infra.sh). SKIP without Grafana.
iamworkbench (AI Workbench gate)The AI workbench admits exactly the roles the access policy compiles, its hub administrators are the policy's and hold only the hub role workbench-admin with exactly the decided abilities (admin page, list and read users, start and stop workspaces, remove hub users), nobody can hold JupyterHub's built-in administrator role (which could create a token for anyone and open their workspace), removing a person from the hub keeps their files, no sign-in tokens are stored, and notebooks cannot reach the platform's private addresses except Keycloak and config-api, compiled from the access policy and only while IAM_POSTGREST_JWT and IAM_DB_ROLES are true.WARN while IAM_GATES is false. FAIL on any difference, or while the hub still runs older settings (run ./infra/deploy-workbench.sh). Also FAIL right after a switch recipe changed IAM_DB_ROLES or IAM_POSTGREST_JWT without its workbench step, or when the workbench was deployed before config-api and the database had both switched: the workbench deploy then opened no route, and running it again fixes it. SKIP while WORKBENCH_ENABLED is not true.
onboardroles (Onboarding roles)The running onboarding wizard admits exactly the roles the access policy compiles (engineer, maintenance).WARN while IAM_GATES is false. FAIL when the list differs or the wizard admits any signed-in account: run ./apps/edge-wizard/deploy.sh when no onboarding run is active. SKIP when the wizard is not running.
pgadminroles (pgAdmin roles)pgAdmin's sign-in admits exactly the roles the access policy compiles (admin), read from the Kubernetes Secret pgadmin-config without printing the client secret, and neither pgAdmin's deployment nor an older copy of it (a ReplicaSet) holds a secret as a plain value.WARN while IAM_GATES is false. FAIL on a difference; while the deployment or an older copy still carries its sign-in settings or default password as plain values (a pgAdmin deployed before 1 November 2026); or when the Secret pgadmin-config is missing: run ./deploy-infra.sh. It does not check that the running pgAdmin has restarted with the Secret's current values. It also FAILs when pgAdmin cannot read its password file /pgpassfile, without which the IoT Postgres entry fails with "no password supplied" (when the check cannot reach pgAdmin's container at all, for example while it starts, it says that instead), and when an address in pgAdmin's list (see the deploy scripts) has no pgAdmin account or no IoT Postgres entry, naming the address; it WARNs while the list is empty. It reads pgAdmin's own database read-only and prints no password.
supersetroles (Superset roles)Superset's sign-in maps exactly the roles the access policy compiles (builders and viewers), read from the Kubernetes Secret superset-secrets without printing any secret; its data connection logs in as svc_superset; its image is pinned by digest; its secret key is set (not Superset's default, at least 32 characters); and neither the deployment nor an older copy of it (a ReplicaSet) holds a secret as a plain value.SKIP while Superset is not deployed, which is every install until a policy version with Superset is applied (on a new install, version 1); the text says when IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is not true. WARN while IAM_GATES is false, while IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is not true (the next deploy stops Superset) and when no Superset pod runs. FAIL on a different role mapping (./apps/superset/deploy.sh --gate-only), a running pod started with another Secret or ConfigMap than the live ones (its medcea/config-checksum: it may still admit an older mapping; ./apps/superset/deploy.sh), a secret as a plain value, a missing Secret, a default or short secret key, another database login, an image without a digest (./apps/superset/deploy.sh), and when Superset runs although the applied policy has no Superset or gives no role a setting (./apps/superset/deploy.sh --gate-only stops it). One of the nine checks apply.sh runs before and after an apply.
backupage (Backups)The newest complete nightly backup in BACKUP_DIR is at most 26 hours old.WARN beyond 26 hours, FAIL beyond 72 or when the folder cannot be read (run the check as the account that deployed the backup); SKIP before ./apps/backup/deploy.sh and on its first day. See Backup and restore.
pvc (Grafana volume)Grafana's volume grafana exists and is bound, so the dashboards Editors make survive a restart, and its directory on this host is mode 700 (Grafana's account only).WARN when it is missing or not bound, or when its directory is open to other local accounts (after a restore, before Grafana restarts): run ./deploy-infra.sh.
noderedflows (Node-RED flows vs git)Every flow node from the repository runs in Node-RED unchanged (layout aside).WARN on flows built only in the editor, or on settings the editor added to a repository node: review them, and commit what should stay. FAIL when a repository node was changed or deleted in the editor, or Node-RED runs no flows at all: run ./apps/node-red/deploy.sh to put the repository's flows back, or commit the change. At least WARN while a file under apps/node-red/flows is not committed to git ("N flow file(s) not committed to git …"): the waiver W1 covers committed flows only, so commit them. The message names nodes, settings and files, never their values.
noderedauth (Node-RED editor rights)Node-RED's own editor sign-in is on, its rights are the ones compiled from the policy, it runs the repository's settings, and its admin interface refuses a call without a sign-in.FAIL on any difference: run ./deploy-infra.sh. FAIL also while the break-glass below is in use, and when the sign-in module could not be installed (the editor then refuses everyone; check the pod's access to the npm registry, then restart Node-RED).
iamenforce (Service enforcement)The shared access settings and every service pod agree with IAM_ENFORCE=true, and IAM_DB_ROLES is true.WARN while false, or when a pod's copy is still true, and when the switches recorded in settings.json (IAM_GATES, IAM_NETPOL, IAM_POSTGREST_JWT, IAM_MQTT_PERSON) differ from config.env ("settings.json switches differ from config.env …": run ./deploy-infra.sh). FAIL when settings.json has no enforce key (the services would read it as false), when the shared access settings disagree with config.env (run ./deploy-infra.sh), when IAM_ENFORCE is true but IAM_DB_ROLES is false, or when a pod's copy is still false under true (redeploy the apps when no run is active).
iammqtt (MQTT person credentials)Under IAM_MQTT_PERSON=true: the broker, its credential sync, the MQTT Explorer page and every running iam-api pod run personal credentials, each iam-api pod with the MQTT rows (mqtt.json) the ConfigMap holds; the LAN port's file holds no personal credential and the WebSocket file nothing else. In either mode: the removed shared mqtt-explorer account is in no password file, and the Explorer page's mode follows the switch (off while false).WARN while false (the Explorer has no credential), naming iam-api if it is not deployed, when the broker's credential sync has not reached the database for over 5 minutes, and when an iam-api pod reads older MQTT rows within 120 seconds of the ConfigMap's last change (the kubelet copies it within that time); after 120 seconds that is a FAIL (./apps/iam/deploy.sh), and so is no running iam-api pod. FAIL when any part disagrees with config.env (the message names the deploy to run), a name is on the wrong listener, or IAM_DB_ROLES is false. It reads usernames only, never a password hash.
jwks (Realm signing keys)The Kubernetes Secret medcea-jwks, from which every service and config-api verify tokens, holds the realm's signing keys: each key id it holds is one the realm publishes, each RS256 key the realm signs with is in it, and jwks-sig.json is exactly the signing keys of jwks.json. It prints key ids only, never a key. It runs whatever the switches say.FAIL when the Secret or one of its two keys (jwks.json, jwks-sig.json) is missing or not a key set, holds no RS256 signing key, when jwks-sig.json is not jwks.json's signing keys, when the Secret holds a key id the realm no longer publishes, or when the realm signs with a key id the Secret lacks (tokens signed with it are refused everywhere): run ./deploy-infra.sh, which republishes the keys. WARN when the realm does not answer (the Keycloak checks report that; the Secret is not blamed) or the Secret cannot be read. SKIP without kubectl. See Troubleshooting for a key rotation.
kcscopes (Keycloak client scopes)The realm has the client scopes groups (with its mapper putting the realm roles into the access token's groups claim) and medcea-identity (with the medcea-api audience and the person_id claim in the access token), and each of the platform's 15 Keycloak clients has both as default scopes. The client list is the one ./deploy-infra.sh attaches the scopes to (infra/lib-keycloak-clients.sh). Keycloak's own database is read in a read-only transaction; no admin token, no sign-in event.FAIL when a scope or one of those mappers is missing, the realm is not in the database, or a client whose tokens reach a platform API (portal, access, policy, config, monitor, scheduler, dbmgmt, mqtt-explorer, edge-wizard, workbench-notebook) is missing or lacks a default scope: run ./deploy-infra.sh. WARN for the same on a client that only signs people in to a tool (pgadmin, node-red, workbench, grafana, superset), for a scope attached as optional only, for a client with full_scope_allowed off, for the audience also in the ID token, for a client-level mapper writing groups, person_id or aud, and when the database cannot be read. SKIP without kubectl.
iamnetpol (Application network policies)Under IAM_NETPOL=true, the NetworkPolicies labelled medcea/iam-netpol=true are by name exactly the set the applied policy compiles, one per application pod. The policies' rules themselves are not compared; tests/iam-network.sh tests what they let through.FAIL under true when a compiled policy is missing (that pod admits any caller in the cluster): run ./deploy-infra.sh. WARN under true for a labelled policy the policy no longer compiles (the next ./deploy-infra.sh deletes it), and always while IAM_NETPOL is false, naming any labelled policies that remain. SKIP without kubectl.

Which check proves what (Phase 5)

Each part of the platform that applies the access policy has a check that proves it runs the applied version, compared with a fresh compile of that version. "Runs the applied version" means the digest the part loaded equals the compile's digest; the version number a pod reports is information only.

Who applies the policyChecks
The six Python services' route table (routes.json)iamartefacts (the ConfigMap is the compile) and iamloaded (every running pod loaded it)
iam-api (the Policy UI and the MQTT credential)iampolicy (its applied version and its compiler) and iammqtt (each pod's MQTT rows)
The databaseiamgrants, iamdbroles, iamchain, and since the second round iamcatalog (owners, triggers that cannot be skipped, views with the reader's rights) and iamanchor (the history's head against the newest backup)
The User Manager and Keycloak's accountsiamdecisions (decisions waiting for qa) and iamdrift (Keycloak's accounts against the account record)
The sign-in proxiesiamartefacts
The tools that sign people in themselvestheir own role checks: grafanarole, iamworkbench, noderedauth, onboardroles, pgadminroles, supersetroles
The brokeriammqtt (the credential sync's freshness)
Token verificationjwks (the keys), kcscopes (the claims every token must carry), postgrest (config-api)
The networkiamnetpol

The rule for FAIL and WARN in these checks (owner decision of 9 November 2026, see the decision record): FAIL only for what lets someone in, breaks token verification, or proves that a pod runs an outdated route table, and (second round, the same day) for what proves the access records were tampered with or drifted: an unexplained role, a failed compensation, a cut or rewritten history, a catalog change that would let a write skip its record; everything else that is not in its final state WARNs.

iamanchor proves only that the history was not cut or rewritten since the newest backup by someone who could not also change that backup (and someone who rebuilds the whole history with a first event newer than that backup gets its "predates this database" WARN, not a FAIL): an account with superuser rights in the database and access to the host could alter both, and a change made after the newest backup and before the next one is not seen until that backup runs. iamdrift needs an access-api from Phase 5's second round: until ./apps/access/deploy.sh has run it WARNs "this access-api predates the drift report". Waivers whose review date has passed or is within 30 days are judged by iampolicy.

IAM test scripts

These scripts check the running platform. Run them from the repository root, or from ./medcea.sh under Health and tests. Each exits 1 on any failure and prints a PASS or FAIL line per item.

ScriptWhat it checksLockGreen looks like
tests/iam-check.shEach of the five Python service pods has the route table, settings and keys mounted, its settings say the same IAM_ENFORCE as config.env, and a forged request sent straight to the pod is caught.No (read-only)Every pod PASS. With IAM_ENFORCE=false the forged request leaves a "would refuse" line; with true, a "refused" line and a 401. The User Manager's admin port and Database Management always refuse.
tests/iam-schema.shThe route table in the ConfigMap and in every pod equals a fresh compile; the IAM schemas and their grants are in place; the hash chain verifies, and an edit to it is refused (in a transaction that is rolled back).No (read-only)Every item PASS. Red right after a pull until ./deploy-infra.sh and ./apps/database/deploy.sh have run.
tests/iam-hosts.shEach signed-in host's live gate admits exactly the roles the policy compiles (for Grafana, the AI workbench, the onboarding wizard and pgAdmin, their own role setting), its 403 page names them, its proxy pod is newer than its configuration, Keycloak accepts its sign-in scopes, and at least one enabled account can open it. For pgAdmin also that it can read its password file and that each listed address has its IoT Postgres entry (SKIP while the list is empty). For Superset (SKIP while it is not deployed): no secret as a plain value, the live role mapping equals the compiled one, the running pod was started with the live Secret and ConfigMap, the sign-in reaches Keycloak with the groups scope, and some enabled account holds a mapped role; and in every case the Keycloak client superset, read from Keycloak's own database: callback only on Superset's address, its sign-out return registered, groups a default scope.No (read-only)Every compiled host PASS; hosts not compiled yet are SKIP with the phase that adds them.
tests/iam-signin.shCreates one throwaway account per role (test-<role>-<random>, e-mail @<project>.example.org, which pgAdmin accepts), signs each in to every gated host as a browser does (the onboarding wizard and pgAdmin included: 12 accounts on 12 hosts; once Superset is deployed 13 hosts, 156 sign-ins, the Superset roles each account gets and whether SQL Lab opens checked too; Superset is skipped while it is not deployed or IAM_GATES is false), and compares who gets in with the policy. Where an account gets in, it calls one read-only API per service and checks the services refused exactly the calls the route table refuses.YesNo mismatch. A refused call answers 401 or 403; an allowed call never answers 401 or 503. The accounts are deleted on exit, also on Ctrl+C. On the AI workbench no workspace is started; the throwaway administrator removes the other test accounts from the hub and stays listed there itself. On Node-RED each editor sign-in must be accepted with exactly the policy's rights and then revoked. When pgAdmin turns an account away for any reason other than its role, the test prints pgAdmin's own message. The Superset users its sign-ins made are deactivated in Superset's database at the end (only this run's; see Superset).
tests/iam-workbench.shCreates a throwaway administrator and a throwaway bio_scientist. The scientist starts a workspace; the administrator must see the hub's admin page and hold the rights of the hub role workbench-admin (which it receives through its hub group, so the test reads the rights it actually holds) and no built-in administrator rights, must be refused (403) at the hub's authorize step for the scientist's workspace (an "Authorize" page there counts as access and fails), must be refused (403) when it tries to create a token for the scientist or change the scientist's hub account, must be refused when it tries to read the scientist's tokens or shares (403, or 404 "not found", which the hub answers when someone holds that right only over their own account), must see no stored sign-in token, and stops and removes the scientist from the hub. Then the scientist's role is removed, and the account disabled: each time a fresh sign-in must be refused.YesEvery step PASS, and the scientist's home folder survives its removal from the hub. The accounts and that home folder are deleted on exit.
tests/iam-mqtt.shNeeds IAM_MQTT_PERSON=true. Creates a throwaway engineer, operator and administrator. The operator gets no MQTT credential; the engineer gets one with the policy's topics, which reaches the broker's WebSocket file within 20 seconds, connects there and is refused on the LAN port; the shared mqtt-explorer account is refused on both. Write rows exist only for units flagged for commissioning without a running run. The administrator then deactivates the engineer in the User Manager: the credential leaves the broker within 20 seconds, and the engineer's old session gets no new one. With --commissioning UNIT (an existing unit with no run running or scheduled) it also creates a throwaway qa account and, through the Configuration UI as a browser, has the engineer flag UNIT for commissioning, checks the engineer cannot approve it, has qa approve it, sees the engineer's write rows for UNIT within 20 seconds, ends it and sees the rows go within 20 seconds; the unit is ended on exit whatever happens.YesEvery step PASS. The accounts are deleted on exit; the deactivation stays in the account decisions, and with --commissioning the proposals, approvals and the policy history's commissioning events stay, all append-only.

tests/iam-signin.sh leaves a Keycloak login event in each test account's name, which stays after the accounts are deleted.

Two offline checks need no cluster: python3 tests/iam-routes-diff.py compares the route table with the routes each service serves (the IAM_ENFORCE recipe runs it with --strict), python3 tests/test_policy.py runs the policy unit tests, and python3 tests/test_config_ui_approvals.py and tests/test_config_ui_commissioning.py check the Configuration UI's approval and commissioning screens (under node, when installed).

Operators and units

An operator works in the units they are assigned to.
